speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The first prong would be to tackle the low-hanging fruit.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In our opinion, some of the shortcomings can be addressed by the Executive Government directly, if it is willing to do so.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second prong will be to commission an external review of the more complex matters concerning our justice system.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These other matters involve other Organs of State and touch on constitutional matters.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My speech and those of other Workers' Party's Members of Parliament or MPs will cover issues on both the low-hanging fruit as well as the more complex matters.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Before I go further, I should declare for the record that I am a lawyer at the firm that has been appointed to represent Ms Parti Liyani in her complaint against the Prosecutors under Legal Profession Act.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, I am not personally involved in handling the matter.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, the Workers' Party is mindful that the disciplinary proceedings are pending.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We will, therefore, not be touching on the conduct of the DPPs especially with regard to the DVD player.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Before I get to the issues with our justice system, let me set the context.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Ms Parti Liyani's case has attracted significant public reaction and we need to ask why.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is it because Singaporeans enjoy the spectacle of powerful people being taken down, or are we energised by the triumph of a domestic worker against the odds?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Captivating as these themes are, the Workers' Party is more concerned about the issues that the case represents.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How far does our system of justice put everyone on equal footing, whether CEO or domestic worker?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Have there been domestic helpers, work permit holders and even poorer Singaporeans who believed that they were innocent but have pled guilty to charges because they did not know their rights or could not afford to fight their cases?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If we are being honest, we should not ask whether there have been such persons but rather how many there have been.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The critical question that Ms Parti Liyani's case has raised is this: how do persons who are disadvantaged navigate the justice system?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is a critical question to ask, as Article 12 of the Constitution provides that all persons are equal before the law and entitled to the equal protection of the law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government has often cited Singapore's high international rankings of our justice system and, indeed, we agree that it has significant strengths.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While the overall ranking over the eight factors assessed is commendable, we should note that Singapore is not ranked so well in a few factors and sub-factors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, on the important factor of constraints on Government powers, Singapore scores have fallen every year from 2015 to 2020.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Singapore is below average as well in two sub-factors here.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Singapore was found to be below average in having effective checks by non-government entities such as media and civil society, and below average in having effective checks by Parliament.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under the factor of open government, the Rule of Law Index ranks Singapore 28 out of 37 high-income countries on the question of whether there are effective complaint mechanisms for citizens.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Singapore is also below average on civic participation which includes the protection of the freedoms of opinion and expression, assembly and association.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The picture for Singapore is thus more mixed than the overall ranking suggests.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We do not take Singapore's achievements for granted.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Singapore is a safe place to raise children and the justice system has been instrumental in achieving that.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are also many public-spirited professionals working in law enforcement, prosecutions and the Courts who take their mission seriously.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Over recent years, the Government has also taken some progressive steps in the right direction.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These include introducing a statutory framework for disclosure of evidence before trial and enabling video recording of suspect statements in certain situations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: By filing this Motion, the Workers' Party is not saying that the system is broken or ineffective, but we believe we should strive to do even better.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is room for improvement in any system.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We believe that more attention should be paid to certain shortcomings in fairness, access and independence which need to be addressed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In this debate, several Workers' Party's MPs will speak.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We will cover the plight of the poor and disadvantaged and offer suggestions on how fairness and access to justice could be improved.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We will review the role, culture and practices of law enforcement agencies, the Courts and the Attorney-General's Chambers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We will examine whether there are any gaps in seeking recourse when things have gone wrong.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We will also argue that enhancing the system in these areas is in the broader national interest.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, the plight of the poor in obtaining justice; second, concerns relating to law enforcement agencies; and, third, justice for crime victims.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, the plight of the poor in getting justice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Our criminal justice system inherited from the British is adversarial.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It involves a contest between competing parties with the judge playing a relatively passive role of evaluating whether each side has satisfied its respective burdens of proof.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is unlike certain justice systems in Europe where judges play an active inquisitorial role and direct parties to investigate before judgments are made.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Our adversarial system requires battle and resources count.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As a law student in the 1980s, I did empirical research on our system.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I sat at the public gallery of the busiest Court handling crash criminal cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The presiding judge handled several hundred cases valiantly with just a minute or two to decide on questions such as whether to grant bail and what amount of bail to set; whether to permit detention of the suspect for investigations and so on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Given the marketplace vibe of the Court, it would be easy to forget that each case involved the rights of persons enshrined in the Constitution.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the cases where the suspect had a lawyer, the Court was given more information to make its decision.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Where the accused was unrepresented, the Court only had the Prosecution's arguments to go on, as the suspect often said nothing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, we still see unrepresented accused persons in front of judges, facing a prosecutor who is state-funded and with deep resources.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is unclear what proportion of persons go through the criminal justice system unrepresented.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These unrepresented persons do not know what to do when prosecutors submit bundles of legal authorities to persuade judges to convict or to fix a sentence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Because of their lack of legal knowledge, some of them inadvertently irritate judges because they say things which are not legally relevant or come across as disrespectful or even under-dressed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In 2007, I filed a Parliamentary Question or PQ about the demographic profile of the prison inmate population.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As those with less education tend to have lower incomes, one can conclude that the proportion of poorer persons in prison is higher than in the general population.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is widely acknowledged that the poor tend to be over-represented in criminal cases globally.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, this phenomenon is not unique to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But why is it that the poor have more difficulties with the criminal law?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, the poor are more likely to fall foul of the law because of their circumstances.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As the French poet Anatole France famously put it in 1894, and I quote, "The law, in its majestic equality, forbids the rich as well as the poor to sleep under bridges, to beg in the streets and to steal bread".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am not saying that the law was purposely enacted to favour the rich but the law does have unintended discriminatory effects on the poor.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Second, when someone is faced with an investigation, there are economic hurdles.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is some legal aid available, provided you satisfy a test of means and qualify for the schemes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Another major concern is, how does one remain free while the case is pending?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On this issue of pre-trial liberty, there has been some research done in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Ms Parti Liyani was fortunate that the NGO Home helped her find a bailor, but many accused persons cannot find bailors of sufficient means.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If one is incarcerated, there is disruption to family income and education, and decreased job prospects.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is also much harder to consult with any lawyer or witness to prepare one's defence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under the Criminal Procedure Code, the Police and the Courts can release a suspect either on bail or on his personal bond, that is, on his own promise to attend Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The majority of suspects are offered money bail and need to find a bailor.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The law states that the amount of bail should be "fixed with due regard to the circumstances of the case as sufficient to secure the attendance of the person arrested or charged".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This may sound surprising, as many of us consider such offence notices as easily settled through prompt payment of composition fines.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But this is not so for those who have insufficient means to pay and have to attend Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The entire household can be derailed by such problems.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Still on the issue of bail, I filed a Parliamentary Question in 2008 on the Bail Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One year on, I asked what outcomes had been achieved.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, it seems that the Bail Court is not heard of.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Has it been discontinued and if so, why?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It also appears from past Parliamentary Questions filed by Members of Parliament, including myself, that statistics on bail are not readily tracked by the Government.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If poorer Singaporeans face significant hurdles, work permit holders such as Ms Parti Liyani face even more.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Work permits can be cancelled any time at the discretion of employers or MOM.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This puts tremendous pressure on work permit holders to cooperate with the authorities and their employers even when unreasonable and legally questionable demands are made.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, in 2008, the Police investigated a case of sexual assault on a University student at Clementi Woods Park.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When I filed the Parliamentary Question on the legal basis for such action, the Minister stated that it was permitted because, "the workers had voluntarily given their consent." I assumed the workers might have signed consent forms but what is the quality of that consent?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: More importantly, what signal is being sent about institutional attitudes?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Why did the Police not ask nearby homeowners to voluntarily give blood samples too?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The disadvantage of the poor has to be juxtaposed with the formidable powers of the state.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Law enforcement agencies are given wide powers of investigation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The defence does not have similar powers to seize evidence or to compel statements from witnesses.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In recent judgments, the Court of Appeal has recognised the disadvantages faced by the defence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If we are not careful, the system could become oppressive for the poor and disadvantaged.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For less serious offences, paying a composition fine enables the offender to settle the matter quickly out of Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If the composition fine is not paid by a deadline, the offender faces a higher penalty in Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This gives a second chance for composition before sending the case to Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some agencies now allow the offender to apply online to extend the payment deadline.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: All these are good moves which we support.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, with composition fines going up, it would be ideal if the agencies could consider allowing instalment payments of fines.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For composition fines, the options can be kept simple.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, a maximum of three instalments with further action if default occurs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such instalment payments will help poorer families cope and prevent cases from snowballing into bigger Court fines, defaults and warrants of arrest.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I earlier touched on the difficulties of the poor in raising money bail.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We need to understand the issue in more depth.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I mentioned that the Government had given answers in the Parliament that it does not collate statistics on the proportion of persons offered bail who do get bailed out.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is a need to regularly collate and publish such statistics, and I ask the Government to do so.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In addition, there is already provision to release a person on his own bond.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If a personal bond is deemed inadequate, alternatives to money bail should be actively considered.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some of the non-monetary methods could include requiring the accused to maintain employment, abide by restrictions on personal associations, residence or travel, to report regularly to a designated agency, comply with a curfew and so on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To get the Police and the Courts to consider such options, the Government could consider amending the Criminal Procedure Code to explicitly require consideration of such non-monetary conditions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That brings me to the end of my first point on the plight of the poor.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In Singapore, whenever questions about criminal justice are raised, public surveys are cited about the high public confidence in law enforcement agencies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I wonder, however, whether persons who have actually experienced the law enforcement process have been surveyed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It would be useful to know the satisfaction levels of crime victims, witnesses and suspects.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Minister has shared the findings on the Police investigations into the Parti Liyani case, together with MHA's initial assessment of what needs to be done.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have some further suggestions on what could be done to raise the bar at law enforcement agencies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I hope that law enforcement agencies do not have a culture of preferring the most serious possible charge against accused persons to leave room for plea bargaining.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If the accused person is unrepresented, there may well be no bargaining.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This will increase the chances that unrepresented accused will receive harsh outcomes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From my past experience, I also observed that some officers believe that showing moderation in the selection of charges might open them up to allegations of corruption.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If such defensive behaviour exists today, it will lead to injustice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As Ms Parti Liyani's case illustrates, problems can arise with interpretation of statements recorded in English.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the past few years, I have come across Chinese-educated residents facing police investigations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They told me that they did not have the competence to check the accuracy of statements recorded in English and had to rely on what the interpreter told them while trying to focus under very stressful circumstances.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When I read their statements and asked them about the incriminating parts, they claimed that they did not utter those words.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When asked why they signed the statements, they said they were unable to check the statements and wanted to complete the stressful process as soon as possible.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Lawyers sometimes see statements with contents that contradict each other.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When statements are challenged in Court, public time and expenses are incurred.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In other words, the text of their statement should be written in the person's first language.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I appreciate that this will involve more administrative effort but the statements will be more reliable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It would be useful to know how much attention is paid to training officers in the skills required to be fair and seen to be fair.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To be an agency accepted by persons of all cultures and socio-economic classes, law enforcement officers need to understand multi-culturalism and guard against inadvertent discrimination.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Are officers sensitised to ensure that they are seen to treat the rich and poor equally?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The final point I would make on law enforcement is on the oversight of law enforcement investigations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Attorney-General's Chambers or AGC may be consulted from time to time during an investigation, as the Minister described earlier.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The AGC is thus an important check on investigation standards.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In cases where the prosecution's case collapses or is found wanting, it would not be fair to place blame exclusively on the law enforcement agencies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As far as Ms Parti Liyani's case is concerned, I hope that the police investigator does not become a convenient scape-goat to pin all the case's shortcomings on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That brings me to the end of my second point concerning law enforcement agencies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Now, let me move to my third area – justice for crime victims.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This was not an issue in Ms Parti Liyani's case.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, the issue of justice for crime victims should be highlighted in any review of the system as crime victims are stakeholders that tend to be sidelined.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have spoken on the issue of justice for crime victims in this House over the years, so let me briefly recap.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Though one of the aims of criminal justice is to pursue justice for victims, the reality is that crime victims have no say in how criminal cases are conducted.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Criminal prosecutions are decided by the public prosecutor or PP, who is the AG.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thus, for instance, the PP will decide which charge to prefer against the offender and may even decide not to press charges at all.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is nothing the victim can do to stop that.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Victims may even suffer damage by the criminal justice process, such as if they are disbelieved by law enforcement or subject to ridicule by lawyers during cross-examination in Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This additional damage inflicted by the system on victims is called secondary victimisation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Countries such as the UK, New Zealand and Australia have legislation protecting the rights of victims as they go through the criminal justice system.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Japan is an active contributor to the field of victimology.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To be fair, there has been some limited progress in Singapore in justice for crime victims.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For many years, the Police have presented victim impact statements in Court to enable judges to hear from victims before sentence is passed on offenders.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, I believe this is limited to a small category of offences such as sexual crimes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Our laws have also been amended to require judges to consider making compensation orders at the sentencing stage, recognising that the victims may have suffered loss and expense.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, I believe more needs to be done to give crime victims confidence that they will be fairly treated by the system.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When victims report cases to agencies, they need to incur time, expense and emotional stress, but they report, expecting that somehow, justice will come out of it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Unfortunately, some were shocked and disappointed at how their cases ended up.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This would have meant that the driver must have violated some traffic signal.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The incident was reported to the Police and she and her family assisted in investigations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, she continues to suffer from the incident not just physically but by having flashbacks and post-traumatic stress disorder.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Her husband saw me and asked why the charge was so light and what they could do about it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In a separate case, a lady contacted me to share her experience when she reported an offence of rape.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: She said that she decided to report it after much pain as she had spent some weeks dealing with the trauma of the incident as well as having an abortion.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: She felt shattered that the system had failed her.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When she wrote to me recently, she mentioned that no reason had been given to her for closing the case and put this question, "Am I not allowed to ask?" Sir, we accept that the state has to take charge of criminal cases to ensure consistency and fairness to accused persons.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, the system would not be able to function if victims do not come forward to assist in criminal cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My colleagues will cover other areas relating to the Courts, the Attorney-General's Chambers, access to justice, complaint mechanisms and why enhancements to justice are in the national interest.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, Sir, what is the Workers' Party calling for?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: There are other areas which are more complex and touch on constitutional matters.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: From my speech, these more complex methods include whether the equal protection of the law under the Constitution is in practice being afforded to the poor and whether there are institutional cultures or subcultures that inadvertently discriminate between the rich and poor.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Other matters to be reviewed by the Government or by the Constitutional Commission will be elaborated on by my other Party colleagues.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: We have seen how legal troubles can derail families who do not have the resources to withstand such trials and tribulations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Today's Motion is not about tearing down the system or discouraging those who work in law enforcement, the AGC or the Courts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: It is about a desire to raise the system to the next level.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: It is about plugging gaps to give everyone the confidence that the system will work for everyone, from CEO to the poor and disadvantaged.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In this spirit, Sir, I beg to move.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, I am very honoured to be here to support my colleague Ms Sylvia Lim in passing this, in proposing this Motion.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The title of this Motion is "That this House affirms that fairness, access and independence are cornerstones of Singapore's justice system" and this is a very key goal of our legal system.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What we hope to have is one where everyone must have access to justice and there must be four key points, pillars to this.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First of all, that the police must investigate based on procedures to the AGC.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Third, the Court, the justices must also establish standards in how evidence should be looked into.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Fourth, the defendant's lawyers have also got a role to play so that we are not just listening to one side of the story.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is a very important channel to ensure that we have a better outcome.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If these four pillars are operating efficiently at the same time, then our justice system can achieve what it sets out to achieve.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Can we allow this access to justice to be enjoyed by everyone?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The larger the building is, the heavier the building is, the more that the stronger these pillars should be.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Can we ensure that the innocent can also enjoy good justice?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Just as my colleague Ms Sylvia, Lim has said, Singapore's justice system within this country and also outside of Singapore enjoys good reputation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is the result of our justices, our officers, legal officers and other participants, all the good work that they have done in enhancing and upholding our legal system.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We have no reason to brush aside the good work that they have done all this while.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Workers' Party is also not insinuating that the legal system is not doing what it is out to do.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, we insist that we must ensure that the justice system must be able to operate in a manner without where no one can face any obstacles today.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must ensure that what we do today will allow the next Liyani to be able to subscribe to justice.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Defence lawyers also face a very unequal system against them.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Only by having a more equal system, can we have a better outcome?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Allowing Singapore's legal system to be able to protect the poor and vulnerable so that the legal system will not just be riding on the backs of the poor and the vulnerable.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, what we are suggesting here includes the investigative procedures of the Police to make it better, including the power of the AG and AGC to raise charges.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: All these procedures and measures will ensure that the victim will also, even though they are vulnerable to also have access to justice under our current system.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: During this course of matter, we also need to ensure that the entire legal system is more equal.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must ensure that enforcement side have the right to do what they need to do to ensure that the victims or rather those who — the perpetrators do not escape justice.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: At the same time, we must be honest with ourselves and review ourselves.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Living in this society, do we feel unease?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Are we willing to accept that this justice system will not make any mistakes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But at the same time we also meet to calibrate very carefully and balance it to make sure that the perpetrators do not escape justice.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must know that if our justice building is built too narrowly or if the the threshold is too high, then not enough people can squeeze into the building or be able to enter the building.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Just as equality must be the principles, the pillars and foundational pillars of the founding of Singapore society, these are the cornerstones of Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must continue to strengthen these four pillars of our legal system and continue to strengthen and expand this legal system to ensure that more people can be covered and protected by our system.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Only when everyone can access to justice and when all the public can see that they can enjoy such justice and that the justice system can be enjoyed fairly by everyone.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Then this country can really build our democracy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These lawyers are there to ensure that the accused persons are aware of their rights and obligations under the criminal justice system and act as their advocates and their cases before the judiciary.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is possible that this figure is significantly higher, if you include accused persons who plead guilty.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Studies, some conducted within the Singapore system, have also shown that unrepresented persons have a significantly greater chance of being convicted and are also more likely to receive more severe sentences upon conviction, raising the risk of miscarriages of justice occurring.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As a concrete example, what would be the chances that Parti Liyani or Portela Vilma Jimenez would have secured acquittal upon appeal if they had not been represented by a defence lawyer?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Some of the more common reasons for accused persons appearing unrepresented include lack of funds and also awareness.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Many of us are familiar with residents stating that they can either not afford a lawyer or that they do not know where to begin to find one for themselves.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: One of the ways in which we should improve access to justice for all will be to enhance existing legal aid.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of choice is a fundamental liberty found in Article 9(3) of our Constitution.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Can we be said to be taking this right seriously if a significant number of individuals who face criminal proceedings are unrepresented?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Presently, only those charge with capital offences are guaranteed to have legal counsel appointed in the form of the Legal Aid Scheme for Capital Offences if they do not have means to engage their own lawyers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is no means test to pass or eligibility criteria to satisfy and the scheme applies to all accused persons, regardless of nationality.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, it appears that the schemes are still limited in their reach, as can be seen by the large number of underrepresented persons and such pro bono legal representation still largely relies on the goodwill of lawyers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, the rights to be allowed to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of choice in Article 9(3) of our Constitution has been qualified by case law, such as Jasbir Singh, a 1994 case of the Court of Appeal that an arrested person is only entitled to consult defence counsel a reasonable time after arrest.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The consequences of this is that accused persons can be held without access to counsel when police investigations are on-going.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is contrasted against other countries, such as New Zealand and Denmark.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In New Zealand, legal aid is available to persons arrested and detained on criminal charges, persons charged with a criminal offence and persons imprisoned on criminal charges.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The legal aid scheme also does not have a set income level in determining the means test but instead adopts a flexible approach by considering various factors, such as a person's gross income for the past 12 months, together with their disposable capital.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In Denmark, the police have a duty to guide an accused person on their option to have defence counsel appointed when provisionally charged in a criminal case.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And in a number of cases, the courts may appoint a public defence counsel for the accused person.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As a general rule, defence counsel must be appointed in all criminal cases, unless the case is minor.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And the cost of appointing public defence counsel is initially paid out of public funds, with such costs to be recovered only upon conviction.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Apart from that, the review we are calling for should also consider automatically providing legal aid to certain groups, such as to all individuals charged with serious non-capital offences carrying long-term imprisonment sentences and do not qualify for CLAS or, in the case of Canada, where legal aid is mandatory for all youth offenders.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The review should also look into how we can ensure that vulnerable segments of society are informed of their rights and where to seek legal aid.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The final topic I would like to speak on today will be in relation to the statutory compensation for miscarriages of justice.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Member for Aljunied has already spoken about compensation for victims of crimes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, I believe the review we are calling for should also look into whether there is scope to bolster the current compensation scheme that we have for accused persons who have been acquitted.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This qualifier does not account for how an accused person still suffers emotionally from having to go through a trial where they stand accused of a crime and that they may also suffer financial losses or loss of income while the charge is hanging over their heads, even if the prosecution was taking it up in good faith.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I just wish to inform Members that I will be moving for us to continue past the moment of interruption.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This case lasted for 4 years, going through all sorts of twists and turns which include the police's handling of the stolen items, the DVD player presented by the prosecutors as evidence in court, and the State Court judge choosing to believe in Carl Liew and convict Ms Liyani.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: All these have aroused a strong sense of justice among many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In their eyes, this is a clash between the rich and the poor.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The rich and famous use their power and the judicial system to take advantage of a vulnerable maid, and the judicial system did not seem to have treated her fairly.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: To be honest, I felt the same way when I learned of the High Court's ruling.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, from the perspective of the general public, I can totally imagine that the ordinary citizens would cheer silently for Liyani’s acquittal and getting her freedom back.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: On the other hand, people also started to have suspicions, frustrations, and even resistance towards celebrities and our legal system.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Therefore, I welcome the statement just made by the Minister for Home Affairs and Law.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is not appropriate for the Minister to make further comments.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But the point is that due process is being carried out progressively.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Third, as for Carl Liew, we learnt from the Ministerial Statement that the authorities have also started further investigations on him.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: At the same time, after further reflection on the case, I begin to understand that precisely because the case has drawn much public attention, we must be more vigilant, and avoid falling into the trap of "knocking off everyone in the boat with one pole".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: When "one bamboo pole knocks off everyone in the boat", It is not only the boat that is overturned, but also the people on board the boat.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, let me first talk about the boat, then talk about the people in the boat.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The so-called "boat" is our country's current legal system.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Liyani case reflected several core issues in the system.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The first question is: does the system work in favour of the rich and powerful?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In 2019, Tay May Li, daughter of the Hour Glass founder, was sentenced to 22 months in jail, for careless driving, drug abuse and possession of drugs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In 2017, Howard Shaw, grandson of movie mogul Shaw Runme, was sentenced to 8 weeks in prison, revocation of all classes of driving licence for 8 years for drink driving.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Earlier in 2012, He was sentenced to 12 weeks' imprisonment for child prostitution.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Huang Guang Tian, the son of a shipping tycoon, was charged with 19 counts of drug abuse, fraud and theft and was sentenced to 3 years and 9 months' imprisonment.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: These cases show that our legal system, from the police investigation, prosecution, to sentencing, does not favour the rich and famous.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The second core issue reflected in the case is: is the judicial system fair to the disadvantaged?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In 2016, there was even an employer who was sentenced to 7 weeks in prison for making false report by wrongly accusing his maid of stealing.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Therefore, I feel the claim that the vulnerable group is disadvantaged in the overall judicial system because of their limited resources, or that the system treats people differently based on their social status, does not hold water.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Volunteers in Jurong told me a case that happened a few years ago.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The resident involved was a former drug offender.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: He was caught by the police one day for possessing sleeping pills and was charged with possession of prohibited drugs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The fact is, however, he was depressed because his mother just passed away, and he went to see a doctor for his depression and got a legitimate prescription from the doctor.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But the doctor happened to have retired and migrated overseas.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: He could not find the doctor to prove his innocence and was about to plead guilty.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: When the volunteers and Members of Parliament in Jurong learned about it, they assisted him to engage a lawyer, and called the doctor back as a witness.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Therefore, our judicial system as a whole is fair, just and equal.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In some ways, there is certainly room for improvement, but we should not overlook the overall fairness and equality of the system.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: One bamboo pole should not knock off everyone in the boat.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Justice and equality are the key words in our National Pledge, and also the basic principles of our judicial system.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: They are the foundation of our country, and are our original intentions of nation building.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In other words, the boat, at the highest level, represents the systems in our country and society.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It can also be said that justice and equality, as mentioned in the Motion, go above the political divide.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: They cannot be discussed along political lines, because they are core concepts that must be acknowledged by the whole Parliament.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: There are many heroes and men of outstanding in the system.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: They perform their jobs dutifully and serve us, navigating the ship.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So I hope to see more public recognition and support for our law enforcement and judicial officers regarding this case.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is a matter of manpower and workload.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: To improve the system, we must first identify the root of the problem, beware of the daily challenges faced by law enforcement and judicial officers, and assist them in their tasks as far as possible.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In his famous Kaifeng Court, he also had four important officers to help him execute his work: Wang Chao, Ma Han, Zhang Long, Zhao Hu, and the resourceful Gongsun Ce and a capable guard Zhan Zhao.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Take a look at our own “Kaifeng Court”.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In our system, we also have many people like Gongsun Ce, Zhan Zhao, Wang Chao and Ma Han.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: They are our policemen, prosecutors, law enforcement and judicial officers.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The more sensational a case is, the more we can see the conduct of some officers, and the more we should remain objective, and cheer for the integrity of our officers.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Otherwise, we will not be one of the safest countries in the world.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Even the famous Justice Bao made some mistakes, as in the Bodyguard Liu Xiaoyuan case.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Whether it is a prince or an ordinary citizen, all are treated alike.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It was under this spirit that Justice Bao upheld justice for the people.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Similarly, our legal system also safeguards the safety and rights of all Singaporeans regardless of their status and wealth.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: With a solid foundation in the judicial system, the authorities will strive for excellence to serve the country and the people better, and allow justice to prevail.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I agree that fairness, access and independence are cornerstones of Singapore's legal system and that the Government should continue its efforts to build a fair and just society.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The legal system should not discriminate based on race, language, religion or economic status.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are, of course, not the only principles that one has to bear in mind when considering a criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: To these, I would add that the chief purposes of a criminal justice system are also to keep a country safe and keep the crime rate down.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: People should not live their lives in fear for personal safety or being victims of crime.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A criminal justice system should have measures in place to prevent recidivism or re-committal of offences as well as processes in place to help reform those who are convicted.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The challenge in designing a criminal legal system, of course, is that one has to carefully evaluate the effects of any proposed changes on these different principles.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Generally, anyone can go out late at night in most parts of Singapore without being worried about personal safety.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many people leave doors unlocked without worrying about break-ins.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While many of us take this for granted, this personal safety we feel is really the result of a well controlled crime situation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Like many other countries, for those with drug-related crimes, there is a higher likelihood of recidivism and of committing other crimes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is why keeping the drug situation under control is of vital importance and why we have always supported the toughest measures against drug traffickers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our criminal justice system is also not one set in stone.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is one that has evolved over time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The only point in which I think I depart a little from my friends is I do not think you need a grand Constitutional Commission to reform criminal law.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Constitutional Commissions are usually to change the Constitution and I do not see any proposals to change the Constitution specifically as yet.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But criminal law reform, I think, is part of the natural process of developing our system.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I will give some examples of how the criminal law has evolved through the natural process of criminal law reforms.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Given the tough penalties we have for offences, I think it is important that accused persons must have a fair hearing process and they should not be unnecessarily detained.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This too is a journey that has taken place over the years and more and more rights and liberties have been given to accused persons.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In 2010, there was a major reform of the criminal law.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The prosecution before this was not required to share details of the case or Police statements with the accused before the trial.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was because it was believed that if the accused was innocent, his story should be consistent at all times and if he tells a different story at the trial, the statement to the Police could be brought up to contradict his account.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was the reasoning for why the system was the way it was before that.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, from the lawyers' perspective, this appeared to be unfair because the defence counsel would be operating without knowing what the prosecution had up its sleeve and needed to get their clients to try and recount what had happened and what they had told the Police.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Where there were inconsistencies that emerged at trial while the accused was being cross-examined, the defendant's lawyers would not be able to take instructions for the reasons for this and whether there was any other explanation for the inconsistency other than, of course, the accused lying.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In this way, it was somewhat analogous to the process that have been in place for a long time for civil cases.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As a final step, the prosecution would share the remaining Police statements of the accused and copies of documentary exhibits.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This allowed both the prosecution and defence counsel to anticipate matters and better reduce the drama in Court.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The 2010 reforms also provided for victim compensation because victims are also an important part of the criminal process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the past, criminal law was largely about convicting those accused of crimes and victims were witnesses in the process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If they wanted personal relief, they may need to commence separate civil proceedings.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Courts always had a discretionary power to order compensation for victims but victims did not have a right to insist on this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If the Court chose not to grant compensation, it had to give reasons for doing so.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This mechanism gave victims a right of compensation, which would save them the cost and emotional energy of a second trial process if they were satisfied with the compensation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Another feature of the 2010 reforms – and this goes to how our legal system looks at rehabilitation – is community-based sentences were expanded.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Prior to this, accused persons had limited alternatives to prison like home detention and probation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What this allowed is it gave the Courts a broader flexibility to give sentences that were more proportional for less serious or less culpable offenders.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This too was enhanced by further reforms in 2018.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A wide range of other reforms that have taken place over the years included safeguards for minors and victims of sexual offences and for accused persons in death penalty cases.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The video recording of interviews was also a helpful step in resolving these concerns because judges would also be able to observe the demeanour and behaviour of the accused.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was for vulnerable accused persons or suspects.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This scheme proved to be useful and was made permanent in 2015.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In 2017, this was expanded to include all young suspects under the age of 16.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are all additional safeguards that have been put in place as our legal system evolves.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This represents our commitment to ensuring that the legal system continues to be one that is fair and just.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A second aspect of this that is of course important and it is access to justice.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the earlier speech, Minister K Shanmugam made clear that we have a very large number of accused persons.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think 66,000 was the number every year – I mean, people who are accused of crime.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Clearly, it is not feasible for the state to fund immediate legal representation for everyone.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, for serious offences, I agree it is important for people to have proper representation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are several schemes in place that do this already.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are of course a series of different aid schemes as well which I think the Minister mentioned.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This includes the Law Society's Pro Bono Services, or LSPBS, the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: All of these are basically cooperative schemes led by the bar but with the Government's support as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If I were to look at many of these specific suggestions that my friends made, I think many of them are worth considering.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If I were to look at many of the specific suggestions that my friends made, I think many of them are worth considering.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The plight of the poor, improvements in the law enforcement agencies process and more justice for victims of crime.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are many good suggestions here which can be taken into account as we evolve the criminal justice system and as part of the normal review process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: To sum up, Speaker, I agree that fairness, access and independence should be cornerstones of Singapore's legal system and the Government should continue its efforts to build a fair and just society.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I do not think the Government should ever rest on its laurels.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think principled and systemic reform should continue as it always has over the years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I do not think we need a Constitutional Committee for this but, of course, this is early in the debate, so my mind is not closed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But I also think it is important for us to acknowledge the good work that has been done so far.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The first of the principles he spoke of was the principle of accessibility which he said and I quote, "should be understood in terms of closing the justice gap, which is a metaphor for the problem of unequal access to justice." He said that there are three dimensions to this justice gap.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: One, a physical gap, that is to say the physical distance between an individual and the institutions of justice.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Two, a resources gap which deters the individual from seeking legal recourse due to concerns over cost.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Three, a literacy gap which follows from lack of awareness about one's legal rights and remedies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: He said that the justice system that seeks to minimise the level of injustice in society must necessarily be interested in closing each of these gaps, thereby enhancing and equalising access to justice.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The issue of resources gap has been much talk about and is a continuing work in progress.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: My colleague the hon Ms He Ting Ru has already touched on this point too.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Chief Justice did not elaborate on the term physical gap.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How an average Singaporean thinks of our Judges is important.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: He or she must of course be learned in law and also in the area of specialisation that he or she is known for.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Beyond pure commercial law and particularly in areas like criminal and family law, the ability of Judges to understand and empathise with the different challenges faced by litigants of different socio-economic backgrounds is critical and can, in my view, bridge this physical gap.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For the next part next part of my speech, I will be talking about Judges selection and training in the State Courts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While in the interest of justice, it was right and good that the High Court has allowed the appeal in favour of Ms Parti Liyani.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We cannot always merely rely on appeals to High Court, righting a wrong done in the Lower Court.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To this end, we should strive for even higher standards in all our Courts and, in particular, in the context of the State Court Judges and Magistrates as they are, after all, critical gatekeepers of justice.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They need to be carefully chosen, have a strong and right sense of mission and have the training and disposition to carry the torch of justice for those whose lives have been entrusted to them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On the issue of selection, the issue of age and maturity of our judicial officers in the State Courts, has been raised in this House on at least two occasions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In 2010, during the debate for the Subordinate Courts (Amendment) Bill, my colleague the hon Ms Sylvia Lim, had asked that then Senior Minister of State of Law Assoc Prof Ho Peng Kee, about requirement that in order for a person to be appointed as a Magistrate, one need only have held a relevant law degree for one year.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: At that time, the powers of Magistrate, including power sentencing has already increased over the years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Assoc Prof Ho Peng Kee had, some years before, expressed similar concern about whether young Deputy Registrar and Magistrate could be able to dispense justice and apply the law appropriately without, and I quote the former Senior Minister of State, "The wisdom that comes from experience in dealing with matters of the world." Having to defend the policy, in reply to the issues raised by Ms Sylvia Lim, Assoc Prof Ho Peng Kee sought to assure the House that despite the low minimum requirements, the practice was to appoint judicial officers who exceeded the minimum threshold of one year.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Notwithstanding previous assurances that past appointments have been made for persons who have exceeded the minimum threshold, is it now the time to review the minimum requirement of one or even three years under section 10?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Would it be prudent now to stipulate higher minimum seniority requirements for judicial officers, especially those handling criminal cases as Magistrates and District Judges?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Perhaps, to have someone more senior like eight to 10 years of post-qualification experience.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In my view, it is extremely important to convince the public that Judges understand the lives of ordinary people and people of different stratas of society.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While I am not advocating that we re-introduce the system of jury here, we must understand why some countries continue to cling onto their jury systems – because it is of fundamental importance to them that decisions on life and liberty are made by juries, composed of members of the public from a cross-section of the population.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Currently, the Legal Service Commission chooses legal officers will be posted from the Ministries or the AGC into the State Court Judiciary and then out again.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While this is a positive move, it still leaves the more junior officers open to posting in and out judicial branch.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The posting could also be to and from postings of DPP or Senior DPP.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This may be preferable to the current system to provide more distance between Prosecutors and those working as Magistrates and Judges.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example to avoid having AGC colleagues, some of them being more senior colleagues, arguing cases before them, knowing that they may well be posted back to AGC again in future.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As the familiar administrative law saying goes, "Justice must not only be done but must be seen to be done." When State Court judicial officers are subject to inter-services postings or rotation, I also wonder whether at the moment sufficient time is given for any judicial officer due to be posted to clear his or her cases without compromising the justice and interest of the parties involved.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: At the onset, when trial dates are fixed, frequently, it may be difficult to dictate the actual length of hearing days required.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many litigants may require more trial days as the cross-examination may take more time than expected.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: What happens when the posting is due soon and a trial may possibly not be completed in time?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can or does the judicial officers seek a delay in his or her posting, in the interests of the justice of the litigants of the case?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If this can be done, the proceedings can still continue fairly for all parties without any pressure on time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Spending more time as a judicial officer, coupled with the right training which can be provided by institutions, such as the Singapore Judicial College, can help to mitigate against factors, such as lacking life experience or lacking sufficient understanding of people from different socio-economic stratas of our society as well as any unwitting misunderstanding or prejudices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Talking about training of judicial officers, it is good to know that training is already being increasingly prioritised.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Singapore Judicial College is a development in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Set up five years ago, it is reassuring to see a unified training champion for the Supreme and the State Courts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It conducts various programmes, including induction programme for newly appointed Judges and judicial officers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: That said, lawyers still observe lopsidedness in cases where the accused person is unrepresented.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, at sentencing hearings, the Prosecutor could be arguing for a particular sentence and submit bundles of authorities for the Judges' consideration.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The poor unrepresented accused person will not know how to react to the submission and frequently just ask for leniency.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The unrepresented accused person has no clue what he should expect in respect of the sentence.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: He or she is likely to get, except maybe some gratuitous information fed to him by the IO.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While working on improving access, we should also consider how we can enhance the ability of our Judges to reduce the effect of disadvantages faced by such unrepresented accused persons in their experiences in Court.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many of the accused persons who are unrepresented comes from the poorer and less educated strata of our society.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These people rely on our judicial officers to mete out decisions and sentences, which will not only be fair to them according to the alleged crimes they are charged for but also bear in mind the handicap they may suffer from not having representation at a time of hearing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To this end, research and training should also include checking against any inadvertent prejudice against the poor or less educated, if that is not already done.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It has also been pointed out in an article and titled "Wrongful convictions in Singapore: A general survey of risk factors", dated 2010 Singapore Law Review by Chen Siyuan and Eunice Chua, and this is reported in Singapore Law Reform Review 28 at pages 98 to 122, that there has been reported cases where Judges made wrong assumptions on witnesses' abilities to recall facts and should be trained accordingly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I believe Ms Parti Liyani's case has evoked such strong and widespread reactions because justice and equality are instinctive values that all Singaporeans believe in and cherish deeply.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim's Motion identifies fairness and independence as cornerstones of our criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Where prosecutorial decisions and processes are concerned, justice demands fairness and independence both in reality and in perception.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is a trite saying in law that justice must not only be done, it must be seen to be done.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Thereafter, I will speak on the bifurcation of the Attorney-General's roles, so that they are held by two persons and not one.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Before getting to this year's cases, let me give some background.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This House passed amendments to the Criminal Procedure Code in 2010, which included formalisation of the criminal case disclosure conference procedure.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Before that, there was no statutory framework for discovery in criminal matters in the State Courts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Prosecutors had overwhelming evidence in their hands compared to the defence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, on many occasions, a previously withheld statement of the accused would be sprung on the defence during trial to impeach the accused's credibility, forcing the defence to throw its litigation strategy out of the window.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: After the framework for criminal discovery was enshrined into law, one Member of Parliament in this House said that this was akin to the criminal justice system "moving out of the dark ages".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This was an excellent development making serious inroads into rebalancing the asymmetries of evidence between the prosecution and the defence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, what I wish to highlight from Kadar is this.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In Court, the prosecution ran the argument that it should have an exclusive and unquestionable right to access evidence and unilaterally decide whether the material was credible and relevant based on its own bona fide exercise of subjective discretion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Court rejected this argument, saying that such a procedure would provide an unacceptably low level of accountability.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, the prosecution conceded that while it had an ethical duty to produce any witness before the Court including evidence inconsistent to its case, it argued that it had no legal duty to do so, citing a judicial precedent in Selvarajan James versus Public Prosecutor.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In that case, the then-Chief Justice Yong Pung How ruled that it was not for the Court but for Parliament to impose disclosure requirements on the prosecution.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even so, the starting point is one of tremendous asymmetries of information between the prosecution and the defence, with the system structurally weighted in favour of the former.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Almost 10 years after Kadar, it is apposite to ask how deeply the prosecution's common law disclosure obligations have been internalised in our criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In Ms Parti Liyani's case, the lack of forthrightness of the DPPs in informing the trial court about the serviceability of the DVD player makes a similar point about fairness in our adversarial system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Crucially, however, it raises the public's eyebrows about our prosecutorial culture.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That is all I will say about Ms Parti Liyani's case as her application against the DPPs and, specifically, their conduct in this matter, is pending.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With that background, let me move on to this year's cases on the prosecution's disclosure obligations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Tellingly, the year thus far has seen a number of judgments that, at first blush, reveal troubling aspects to the prosecution's approach to disclosing statements to the defence in spite of the almost decade-old Kadar judgment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One significant case was Public Prosecutor versus Wee Teong Boo, hereinafter referred as Wee Teong Boo.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In that case, the accused, a doctor, was convicted of outrage of modesty and sexual assault.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He faced a total of 10 years' imprisonment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In Wee Teong Boo, the Court of Appeal restated the prosecution's obligation to disclose material, as this can assist the Court in determining the truth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Court referred to a 1916 English judgment, which referred to public prosecutors as "ministers of justice", even as the Court of Appeal confirmed that it is neither the prosecutor's duty to secure a conviction at all costs nor, quoting Kadar's case, to timorously discontinue proceedings the instance some weakness is found in the case.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But non-disclosure revelations in cases like Wee Teong Boo risk crystallising such a public perception.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, judicial decisions on failures of the prosecution to meet disclosure requirements can easily cause the public to lose trust in the Attorney-General's Chambers and by extension, the criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Nabill points to a clear recognition by the Court of Appeal of the central role of disclosure by the prosecution in a fair and just criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Yet another case was reported in the mainstream media only last week.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In this on-going case, a defence lawyer argued that the conviction of an accused person ought to be ruled unsafe because the prosecution did not disclose material evidence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Defence in this particular case had earlier filed a criminal motion in the High Court.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The prosecution in its submissions in Nabill paradoxically makes the argument for legislation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Tellingly, in that case, the prosecution submitted that it may not, despite acting in good faith, fully appreciate the defence that the accused intends to run and, as such, the prosecution admitted that it might, and I quote, "inadvertently fail to disclose statements which might tend to support the defence".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Court of Appeal considered this position as, I quote, "an intolerable outcome".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The inadvertent failure, and I stress, not failure, but inadvertent failure to disclose by the prosecution may be better appreciated if we remember the adversarial nature of our criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some defence counsel and deputy public prosecutors can be far more adversarial than others, and this structure reality and such human factors are potentially a barrier against more consistent standards of the prosecution's disclosure obligations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, the judgments in Kadar and Nabil require that the prosecution actively considers, on an on-going basis, its disclosure requirements.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In view of the human factors alluded to earlier, can consistent standards of disclosure represent a reasonable expectation of the prosecution's obligations, as it would naturally be more substantively focused on its own case, especially during a trial?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I make this point not to run down the prosecution or imply that they are likely to fall short in their disclosure obligations more often than not.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But even so, Mr Speaker, a perhaps overly sanguine expectation of consistent disclosure standards combined with the reality of inadvertent non-disclosure, as admitted by prosecutors today, make it entirely plausible that we could see more future cases of non-disclosure that prejudice the defence, if a decisive legislative move is not made.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At minimum, an amendment to the CPC to codify the prosecution's disclosure requirements, as established in Kadar and Nabill, would send a powerful signal that prioritises proactive and early disclosure by the prosecution at the pre-trial stage when the case for the prosecution is filed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would imbibe greater confidence into the criminal justice system by virtue of far fewer miscarriages of justice arising from non-disclosure.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, if the Ministry is minded to consider a legislative amendment to the CPC, it would be worthwhile to seek the inputs of the Criminal Bar and the Attorney-General's Chambers on the ambit of documents and other material that should be made available to the defence, in the interest of justice.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2010, the Minister argued against criminal disclosure by stating that disclosure of witness statements went against public policy considerations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would be worthwhile to review the extent of disclosure that would serve the ends of justice.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In my opinion, Sir, more disclosure in criminal matters cannot be a bad thing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would allow the Court to have a fuller picture of the circumstances of an alleged crime, with all the relevant evidence marshalled and admitted before the Court from both sides before deciding whether to convict or acquit an accused.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such a regime could also contribute to a more efficient justice system with defence lawyers in a better position to advise on the prospects of success at trial.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A decision by the defence to plead guilty early, for example, would save the prosecution time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
