text: More disclosure could also lower the prospect of cracked trials where the accused pleads guilty shortly after trial begins, but after significant time and resources have already been spent by the prosecution in trial preparation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My second suggestion goes to levelling the playing field for the defence, not for its own sake but to further the interests of justice.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Under section 259 of the CPC, statements of witnesses are not admissible in Court unless specific conditions have been met.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have been reliably informed that in cases where the prosecution adheres to its disclosure obligations, it objects to the admission of a disclosed witness statement favourable to the defence during trial, as it is entitled to do under section 259.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Simply put, the prosecution's position is that if the defence wants to use the contents of a favourable statement, it should get the witness to give evidence in Court, so that the evidence can be tested.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: From a legal point of view, this is a sound argument.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In practice though, it is not as simple as it sounds for the defence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Before calling a witness, defence counsel would, understandably, want to interview that witness.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But what if the witness refuses to cooperate with the defence?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The option is open to subpoena the witness but the defence may not want to subpoena a witness if it has not had a chance to interview the witness, to assess the probative value of putatively favourable evidence against its prejudicial effect.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As it stands today, even with a favourable witness statement in hand, the defence is effectively playing Russian roulette should it choose to subpoena a witness without being fully apprised of the facts and circumstances that led to the making of what the prosecution regards as a favourable statement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In extremis, an unwilling witness may turn hostile on the stand.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This ought to be considered, so as to reassure witnesses, and for the defence to clarify their statements before trial.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Thereafter, the defence can decide whether to call the witness to Court.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The counter-argument against allowing the defence to interview witnesses is that the authorities and the prosecution should not be burdened with such a request.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: After all, in civil cases, the same considerations come into play for counsel.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The difference is that we are not speaking of civil cases here.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In criminal matters, the requirement for the prosecution to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, the demands of natural justice and the importance of getting at the truth of a matter in Court, notwithstanding the adversarial system, requires higher thresholds of fairness than in civil cases.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A system that contributes to a thorough evaluation of the evidence, not just for the prosecution but the defence as well, would strengthen the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As reforms to the criminal justice system are an on-going process, I hope the Government can look into the matter of codifying the prosecution's disclosure requirements and the extent to which what further disclosure requirements are to be made in the name of fairness and to achieve the ends of justice.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This was also raised by Ms Sylvia Lim at the Committee of Supply Debate this year on the Attorney-General's Chambers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Additionally, this was proposed by no less than a former nominated Member of this House, Prof Walter Woon, who served as the fifth Attorney-General of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He persuasively argued for such a separation in an opinion piece published in The Straits Times in September 2017.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But we raise this matter again for the Government to reconsider its position and consider how the current system can be improved, and it is timely to raise this again in light of this Motion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In support of my call, I will make three points.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, there are gaps and blind spots in the current prosecutorial structure; second, improvements should be made to strengthen the system both in reality, as well as in public perception; and third, there are no robust reasons, I would offer, for all the roles of the Attorney-General to be held in one person.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My first point is that there is a weakness in our prosecutorial structure.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Our current structure has two key characteristics that taken together, represent an area where the system can be strengthened.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One, the AG is entrusted with two roles.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The first is that of being the Government's legal advisor and the second is that of public prosecutor.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As the Government's lawyer, the AG takes charge of three areas: legislation, international affairs and civil matters involving the Government, including lawsuits.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As public prosecutor, the AG is to prosecute without fear or favour.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Each of these characteristics may or may not be a weakness in itself.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But it is the combination of both these two characteristics that can compromise the systems foundation in some cases.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As the Government's legal advisor, the AG's duty is to protect the interests of the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is not difficult to imagine cases where the role of the Government's legal advisor conflicts with the role of the public prosecutor.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Say the employees of a Government-linked company pay bribes in order to secure contracts overseas.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Under the Prevention of Corruption Act, extraterritorial corruption is punishable in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, prosecuting these employees which has to be in open court is likely to bring with it negative publicity against the Government of the day in the local and international news media, simply by virtue of the company being Government-linked.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And AG might believe in all sincerity that the interests of the Government are better served by not prosecuting the employees, and as public prosecutor, then decides not to prosecute.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Clearly, the roles of the Government's legal advisor and the public prosecutor are in conflict.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Another example – say a suspect has been arrested for an offence while in custody.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He suffers a serious injury either through a assault or negligence that puts him in hospital.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If this suspect is eventually charged in open court, this is likely to bring with it negative publicity against the government of the day in the local and international media.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And AG might believe, again in also all sincerity, that the interests of the Government are better protected and better served by making a deal not to prosecute the suspect in return for the suspect not suing the Government in Civil Court.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even if an AG can mentally separate the roles and prosecute regardless of the negative consequences to his client, the Government, the fact is that a conflict exists.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We should have a system where the basis of such conflict should as far as possible not even arise.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Again, some scenarios are not hard to imagine.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Say in the future, a Prime Minister installs an AG who is friendly to him.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the time of the appointment by the President, there is no reason to suspect anything untoward about the AG.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Then, the Prime Minister commits serious offences, perhaps acts of corruption.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Despite clear evidence, the AG decides not to prosecute the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This could be due to pressure of desire to keep his job, for favours or simply because the Prime Minister and the AG are cronies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Potential abuse and the pressure on prosecutors is not the stuff of fiction, but a real prospect.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Prof Woon in his opinion piece, says that a look at the state of the world shows that the pressure on prosecutors is common.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are too easily available examples or perhaps I should call them cautionary tales.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will not say more except to say that one is a close neighbour and the other is a major country that regularly makes the news because of its President.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Both these countries have had prominent cases of their Attorney-Generals being subject to political pressure.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They are both instances of how the system can become compromised rapidly even in countries that pride themselves on the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Let Singapore not be one such country in future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I now move to my second point on this subject.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What improvements should be implemented to strengthen the independence of the public prosecutor, both in reality and in the perception of the public?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I mentioned two characteristics in our system that contribute to the problem – the dual role of the AG, as Government lawyer and public prosecutor, and his absolute discretion in prosecutions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As it is the combination of these two characteristics that contribute to potential conflict, a number of changes can possibly ameliorate the prospects of abuse.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Neither role should be subordinate to the other and different offices should be formed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even if no other change is made, this single change removes the possibility of a conflict of interest when one person performs both roles.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Prof Woon says that the prosecutorial function must be held by the Attorney-General as the AG has the necessary stature being second only to the Chief Justice in the hierarchy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He says that the role of being Government legal advisor which involves handling civil matters, international matters and legislation, could be given to the Solicitor-General, for example.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party is open to these views.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, while the splitting of roles takes away conflict of interest, it may not be enough to entrench the independence of the public prosecutor.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Prof Woon suggests a term of five years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: His reason is that this promotes stability in office.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such an individual can of course be considered for the role of Government legal advisor.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, it would be natural for a former elected Member of Parliament to have imbibed the political views of the party he or she used to represent.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even if a public prosecutor who was previously a Member of Parliament does his or her sincere best to be objective, they cannot but help be a product of their previous beliefs, which they perhaps still hold.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A public prosecutor who was a Member of Parliament of a political party and steeped in the party's ideology for years, is likely to hold certain beliefs and approach things in certain ways.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, if there is no connection between the public prosecutor and the Government in power, this engenders greater faith among the public that the prosecutorial system is fair and conducted without fear or favour.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Another aspect to this is that even if a public prosecutor is completely objective and able to divorce himself from his previous political loyalties and beliefs, it is possible that the public may not believe it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is especially so in light of the internet and the easy accessibility of the Member of Parliament's political views when in party politics.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even if there is objective independence, is their perceived independence?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is a clear indicator that the Attorney-General's Chambers and the current Attorney-General himself recognised that the public cares about independence and that public perception matters in reinforcing the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On the matter of the political affiliation of the AG, the Government's position was that in many first-world countries, the AG was a political appointee and that these countries had deemed such a system to be perfectly proper.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, there are many things that Singapore does differently to deliver effective and robust outcomes in light of unique local circumstances.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The political dynamics, competitive political systems, and the limits to political terms, in many first-world countries also operate to represent a check on political appointees.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Ours has been a one-party dominant state for more than half a century.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, the point of an independent public prosecutor free from political links would in fact buttress the rule of law and remain in step with the continued development of an autochthonous legal system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Of course, Mr Speaker, no matter what is done to entrench independence, there will always be someone who is dissatisfied or will imagine conspiracies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But in law, we invoke a reasonable person who in more misogynistic times, was the reasonable man.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What level of independence would satisfy a reasonable person?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this, what I would forward, Mr Speaker, is that the current system can be reviewed and improved against the prospects and perceptions of non-independence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To strengthen the system, the public prosecutor should have criminal justice experience, whether as a prosecutor, defence counsel or judicial officer.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Again, public perception that the public prosecutor is qualified for the job is critical.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While this may not always be possible in all cases, a commitment to criminal law and a deep desire to understand and master it is critical.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Senior Minister of State for Law, as he was at that time, Minister Edwin Tong responded.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The implied conclusion was that it is not necessary to split the roles.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At no point did Minister Tong say either why it is a bad idea to split the AG's roles or why it is preferable for the roles of the AG to be held by the same person.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: From the perspective of justice and independence, there is only upside.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The only reason I can think of for the roles of the AG to be held by one person is that somehow, we lack sufficient legal talent in Singapore to find two people to fill the roles of the Government's legal advisor and public prosecutor.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, that is unlikely to be the case.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Right now, in the Attorney-General's Chambers, there is an Attorney-General, two Deputy Attorney Generals, the Solicitor-General and a Deputy Solicitor-General.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the Deputy Solicitor-General heads the Legislation Division, there is also a Chief Counsel who leads the Civil Division and the Director-General who heads the International Affairs Division.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Let us think of our justice system as a house which has served as a family home.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The house may have stood firm for decades and the occupants may have lived safely, but there is a flaw in the foundations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We were extremely fortunate that Ms Liyani’s counsel Mr Balchandani had an unwavering conviction to ensure that justice was done, and the High Court caught those errors and reversed them, thus preventing a miscarriage of justice.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While it is of absolute importance that both MHA and AGC conduct their own internal investigations, it is frankly not enough.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are three main points of concern with merely conducting an internal review.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are they independent enough to be completely objective in their review?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the wake of the two consecutive breakdowns in December 2011, then Minister for Transport Lui Tuck Yew convened the COI which ran in parallel to SMRT and LTA’s own internal investigations as concerns were raised about possible systemic shortcomings.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I quote the former Minister, “LTA and SMRT have also started their own separate internal investigations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Both parties clearly have the duty and responsibility to find out what went wrong, especially for those areas that they are accountable for… The COI on the other hand is an independent party appointed by the MOT and will also look into the larger systems issues beyond that which SMRT and LTA will cover in their respective probes”.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Compared to the MRT case, the systemic failure in the Parti Liyani case needed even more coordination in order to be addressed because it is not restricted to one Ministry but also involved the AGC and the State Courts.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, it is appropriate to reiterate that justice must not only be done, but it must also be seen to be done.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An internal review by the relevant agencies alone, is unlikely to assuage those doubts amongst our citizens, nor that justice was seen to be done.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans like to know why a simple theft case involving an underprivileged in our society has taken four long years to see the light of day.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The time and resources required in our criminal justice process means that the odds are stacked heavily against the underprivileged in our society.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How can we improve the access to justice for these people?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Although the legal process is based on evidence, Singaporeans are also looking for answers as to why there was little compassion shown to the underprivileged in our society.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Especially in this case, both parties were on opposite ends of society, one party living in the highest echelons of society and the other the complete opposite.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In his appeal judgment, Justice Chan Seng Onn has also raised some questions about the plaintiffs’ motive in filing their Police report.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So it is not just the lack of compassion but there is also a perception of favouritism among some segments of Singaporeans, where the rich and powerful can directly or indirectly enjoy the power of the state to their benefit.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As Han Fook Kwang put it, “People can accept huge differences in wealth, say, between a business tycoon and his servant.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   The Singapore Progressive Party calls on the Government to set up an independent committee of inquiry as soon as possible for further investigation if there are systemic problems in our criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Internal investigation by the various criminal justice agencies are not enough to restore people's confidence in the impartiality of the Judiciary.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans do not understand why a seemingly simple theft case involving a person belonging to the vulnerable group took more than four years to see the light of the day.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The effect that there are so much resources are needed to go to Court means that our judicial system is unfair to the disadvantaged group.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have to give the disadvantaged a fairer chance.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Despite the fact that the law is based on procedures and evidence, it is difficult for Singaporeans to understand why our legal system is almost completely unsympathetic towards the disadvantaged groups.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In particular in the Liyani's case, parties are at an extreme opposite of the society, with one party at the highest echelon of society and the other at the lower end.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In his judgment, High Court Judge Chan Seng Onn also expressed doubts about the motive of the plaintiff in reporting the case.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This had led many to suspect that our system is only lacking in compassion but also that the rich and powerful may use the power of the State to seek welfare for themselves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, we must do all we can to dispel these doubts.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As Han Fook Kwang said that people can accept huge welfare between a business tycoon and his servant because it is reality in Singapore, a capitalist country.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But if there is a gap of privileges beyond this welfare between the rich and the poor which separates the elites from the people, then the people will definitely revolt.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In pursuing these goals, we should address shortcomings and blind spots in our current institutional matrix of laws, regulations, policies and practices relating to justice.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Parti Liyani's case has raised the question of wider access to the criminal justice system and avenues of redress on the part of those with lesser means.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: An ombudsman would provide access to an independent public office with remit and resources to investigate potential wrongdoing, errors, lapses or weaknesses in the conduct of public officials.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The office of the ombudsman would be open to Singaporeans of all backgrounds and income profiles.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The remit of the ombudsman in our proposal would extend to the conduct of all public servants, including the Police and the prosecution service.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In so far as the Police are concerned, this role has parallels with that of independent Police Complaints Commission's or councils found in other jurisdictions, such as the UK and Hong Kong.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, the ombudsman would not have the authority to investigate complaints against the Judiciary so as to protect the vital tenets of judicial independence from any potential or inappropriate external interference.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The idea has in fact been debated publicly and in this House on many occasions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Government then responded that it was not rejecting the proposal but that it was not the right time to institute it.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This was in the 1960s because citizens had not yet developed a clear understanding of their rights and obligations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: According to then Law Minister, Mr EW Barker, such an institution would be, and I quote, "flooded by complaints by people who do not know what are the limits of his jurisdiction".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In 2011, then Member of Parliament and now Leader of the Opposition, Mr Pritam Singh, called for the establishment of an ombudsman during the debate on the President's Address, noting that former President, Mr Tony Tan, had revived interest in this during the presidential campaign.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Mr Singh asked a Parliamentary Question in 2012 as to whether the Government will consider whistle blower protection legislation and the institution of a national ombudsman to act as a layer of deterrence against wayward civil servants.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In response, then Deputy Prime Minister Mr Teo Chee Hean stated that there are multiple channels for raising irregularities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Independent bodies, like the Public Service Commission, the Auditor-General's Office and CPIB are involved in the process.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I shall attempt to summarise these in the following three points.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Having access to such a check would, in fact, bolster the standing of the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, an ombudsman may uncover policy gaps or institutional shortcomings that are not related purely to corruption, accounting or corporate governance that are dealt with by the CPIB and Auditor-General's Office, as I argued in Parliament in 2018.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The office of the ombudsman could therefore table a review paper every year analysing in aggregate, the cases it had dealt with, describing any systemic patterns discerned and putting forth evidence-driven recommendations for systemic change in how the Public Service interfaces with citizens.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In 2016, during the public discussion on the Constitutional amendment to the elected presidency scheme, scholar Mr Chirag Agarwal published an op-ed essay outlining outlining how an ombudsman could benefit Singapore, and I think it is worth citing that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To paraphrase, he argued firstly, the delivery of public services has become more complex and citizens have become more demanding.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Parliament has had to address specific incidents involving Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: An ombudsman should be able to investigate such incidents in the first instance and recommend corrective action where necessary while the Government focuses on developing sound public policy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Government could then consider any policy recommendations made by the ombudsman in its annual report.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And thirdly, the transparency and independence of the ombudsman will help build trust in the Government.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Sir, I would like to consider examples of other jurisdictions that have created the office of an ombudsman or its equivalent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is the OECD, the club of more developed economies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A 2011 report by the Asian Development Bank or ADB noted that most Asian Ombudsman Association or AOA members focus on the following mandates.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Two, addressing systemic issues to improve public administration.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The ADB report noted that an ombudsman can be established either under the Constitution by statute or administrative regulations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some relevant Asian AOA member institutions of interests and their legal basis includes the Ombudsman of Indonesia created under presidential issuance decree number 44; the Ombudsman of Hong Kong created under the Ombudsman Ordinance in 1989; Malaysia's Public Complaints Bureau created under administrative circular number 4 in 1971; the Philippines Office of the Ombudsman created under the 1987 Constitution Republic Act.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Established in 1989, the Ombudsman in Hong Kong monitors public governance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The office strives to improve the quality of public administration and enhance the culture of service through independent objective and impartial investigation into complaints received and by self-initiated studies in Hong Kong.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The office of the Commonwealth Ombudsman in Australia safeguards on aims to safeguard the community in its dealings with the Australian government.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is responsible for ensuring that the actions of agencies are fair and responsible by: (a) handling complaints; (b) conducting investigations; (c) performing audits and inspections and (d) encouraging good administration.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The office of Commonwealth Ombudsman was created by law in 1976 in Australia.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Act provides that the Ombudsman is to investigate the administrative actions of Australian government departments and agencies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Ombudsman interestingly is also the law enforcement and ombudsman and can investigate complaints about the actions of the Australian Federal Police or AFP, and about the policies, practices and procedures of the AFP as an agency.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If a person is dissatisfied after making a complaint to the AFP, they can make a complaint to the Ombudsman.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The classical model is that of an office with extensive powers to investigate cases, question witnesses and requisition documents, one where the ombudsman may work towards mediation of conflicts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If no solution can be reached, they will provide recommendations to the relevant administrative unit.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In this model, the office would have no power of coercion and can only apply soft pressure to get the recommendation accepted.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The ombudsman would submit an annual activity report to Parliament.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, in other words, the model for an ombudsman could be as follows: the office investigates all complaints using an objective process of fact-finding.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The office of the ombudsman would then recommend follow-up action to the public sector agency concerned.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If the follow-up action is not undertaken to a satisfactory extent, the ombudsman would have recourse to the Courts or would have other means of recourse, such as publishing its findings, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The ombudsman would be appointed by Parliament for a fixed term and would be answerable to Parliament.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The office of the ombudsman could be enshrined in the Constitution in an Article that could also specify the grounds for disqualification.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such an Article on disqualification could be modelled on Article 72 of the Constitution for the Presidential Council for Minority Rights or the mechanism for the removal of Judges under Article 98(3)(iv).

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I should stress that this is one model for constructing such an office that seems to me to be reasonable but the question of the operating model for an ombudsman warrants far deeper scrutiny before an appropriate model is defined.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Sir, I would like to deal with objections to the idea of an ombudsman.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I shall attempt to deal with these objections one by one.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: First, we have the possibility of internal reviews within Ministries and Statutory Boards.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But as I mentioned earlier, these would risk not being seen as independent and thus potentially leave open the possibility of a growing trust and confidence deficit.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Second, we have the citizen's right to sue the Government in Court.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, most citizens in Singapore believe that this avenue of redress comes with considerable, if not, prohibitive cost, in terms of money and time, and they believe this for good reason.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Citizens will first have to find a law firm willing to sue the Government and face the AGC as an opponent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, if it is a judicial review action, leave of Court to commence such an action must first be obtained and only then can action be brought.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, two sets of legal costs are involved in a judicial review action.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Third, many documents are in the Government's possession and these may be denied to a litigant due to a claim of official secrecy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: All these factors, taken together, explain the rarity of such legal action.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, the PSC does have powers to conduct investigations into misconduct by public servants, but only on a complaint by a Permanent Secretary as relates to sections 3 and 4 of the Public Services Disciplinary Proceedings Regulations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This means that PSC cannot conduct investigations and complaints brought by members of the public.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Fourthly, we have REACH but REACH again is not an investigative body that can probe the actions of public servants and provide closure in a way that is seen as independent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Fifth, we have the Auditor-General's Office or AGO but the work of the AGO is primarily focused on the annual audit of public sector which involves randomly selecting agencies for audit checks on a sample check basis as auditors do.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: No doubt the AGO can be ordered to conduct off-cycle special audits.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, Sir, the AGO is currently not set up to field the broad complaints about public sector lapses, errors or poor quality of service.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Sixth, we have the CPIB but the CPIB only investigates and resolves allegations of malfeasance, corruption and so on, which are potentially criminal offences, not oppressive, unfair or rude behaviour by public servants, for example; or flaws in the complaints handling process, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It has been a hallmark of our system that Members of Parliament write letters of appeal to Government agencies to address the grievances of constituents.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But, Sir, these appeals are subsequently addressed by the agencies themselves.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The process does not amount to an independent investigation by an external agency, resourced and qualified to do the same.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Members of Parliament's letters merely present the perspective of the constituent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, Sir, let me address the objection that creating an office of the ombudsman will incite a flood of frivolous complaints against public servants, consuming enormous resources and sparking the growth of a complaint culture that may undermine confidence in the Public Service and induce public servants to do their work defensively, as it were.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One can discern echoes of such an argument in the response of former Law Minister, Mr EW Barker to the idea of an ombudsman in the 1960s.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Considering this argument more closely, one can see that this is an argument against creating responsive complaints handling processes of any kind rather than being an argument specifically against the institutional form of an ombudsman.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If we are worried about the system being flooded with frivolous complaints, ought we not to similarly abolish Quality Service or QS departments in Ministries, for example?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Why does an ombudsman risked triggering a flood whereas these other institutional forms of complaint handling do not?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, if a flood of complaints is occasioned by the creation of an ombudsman as it were, might that not be proof that there were latent grievances that members of the public hesitated to bring forth reasons of lack of confidence in existing channels of redress?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If a reasonable fraction of those latent or pent-up grievances turn out to be legitimate, would addressing them not be a good thing for the quality of justice and fairness in our social fabric?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Member will be reminded he has 20 seconds left.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   Fairness is one of the key foundations of our society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is etched in our pledge as Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This democratic society is built on the basis of justice and equality.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We were raised with these values and they are entrenched in us.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Therefore, when something that goes against these values happens, we will reject it and our people will voice it out.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Recently, the Ms Parti Liyani's case has received a lot of attention and made people voice their concerns.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This case involved a helper and her previous employer, Mr Liew Mun Leong who is from a well-to-do family.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One issue that has arisen in the minds of many people is whether someone with a high position in society, like Mr Liew, had used his status to influence our justice system.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many questioned whether our justice system, which encompass the police, the Attorney-General's Chamber (AGC) and the Court, is truly fair and treats everyone equally.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have seen many news materials, sharing of opinions and comments about this case in the traditional media and social media.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Maybe not everyone knows each detail of this case or had the opportunity to read all 100 pages of the written judgment of the High Court judge, but many were affected by the issue of fairness that was raised.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: When doubts were raised about the system and processes in our institutions arising from the decision of the High Court judge and the public concerns in this matter, the Government took steps to investigate further.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This reflects the transparency of the Government and our commitment to fairness.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Minister Shanmugam, from when this case was first raised, had already stated that we have to find out what happened, how it happened and later deal with it; and take responsibility.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: He said that it was the best way to build people's trust towards our system.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: After that, he said, we should disclose the steps that we have taken openly after the review is completed.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Earlier, Minister Shanmugam had analysed in detail the specifics of this case.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: He gave a report on the findings of the investigation that was carried out and answered Members' questions regarding this matter.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There was no evidence that showed any personal relationship between the Liew family and the police, the AGC or the judge.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The police and prosecutors actually considered this case as a routine case such that the superiors were not aware of this case while it was in progress.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The reality is that, specifically for this case, there is no basis to say that there is unfairness or wrongdoing in the judicial process.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The question now is whether the issues of justice and fairness are systemic, are we seeing wrongdoing that is happening pervasively in our justice system?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Is our justice system broken to the extent that we need a review?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On this, I would like to raise a few matters.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The cases that are shown by the media usually have elements that are sensationalized, but when you look at it deeper, there are good explanations that are given, like the Parti Liyani case that we discussed earlier.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If we follow the explanation that is given whenever a controversy is raised, we can see the reasons why a certain decision is made.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In general, we can say that the cases do not raise any issues or show pervasive unfairness in our system.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I was a lawyer specialising in civil and divorce cases.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The clients that come to see me for help come from different backgrounds.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Sometimes my client has to face a big company represented by a big firm.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, in my experience, the judge does not look at someone’s financial ability or skin colour and is always fair.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Each party is given the opportunity to present facts and evidence.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I still remember, a few years ago, our client was a lady who had lost her husband.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Her husband, a motorcyclist, was hit by a bus and later passed away.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We made a claim against the bus driver and the bus company which were represented by a bigger firm.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, that was not a barrier to getting a fair trial.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I was affected by that case because as we were going through the Court process, at one time, the woman became emotional and stated that she did not want any compensation but she wanted the other side to return her husband.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It was sad to watch her situation but fortunately, the case was resolved.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Winning or losing does not depend on someone’s life status and a decision is made based on the truth, what took place and the prevailing laws.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The justice system is indeed blind; it does not look at whether a person is rich or poor, man or woman, and it does not look at your race or religion.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, it cannot be denied that there is a worry that if someone cannot afford it, he cannot get the advice and legal representation and this would affect his ability to present the best case to the judge.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: He may also be hampered by legal processes which are complicated and which he does not understand.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many lawyers are actually volunteers and there are many schemes to help those who have legal problems.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Aside from that, the Court processes are often updated and simplified so as to reduce legal costs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Of course, we should continue to improve the existing help channels.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I had highlighted this issue in my past speeches in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe that this is a work in progress.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But I feel that it is important for us to acknowledge that there are processes and channels for help in our current system.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One more matter that I would like to highlight is the hope and desire of our society to see justice and fairness in all aspects of our lives, not just in Court.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We will feel angry if we see discrimination happen at the work place.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We will voice our unhappiness if we see a group in difficulty that is not being helped.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We do not want to see anyone in Singapore left behind.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Like I said earlier, there are certain values which are entrenched in our society and these values shape our way of life in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Because of this, many systems in our country exist based on our values.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If we see someone needing help, there is a help channel, for example through the Social Service Office (SSO) that we can refer to.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Indeed, there are many efforts and programmes created to ensure that the needy groups are supported to have a better life.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The open discussion today also reflects the efficacy of our systems.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The debate in this Chamber shows the maturity of our society and the existence of space to voice opinions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If our systems are broken and fairness and independence do not exist, today’s discussion could not have happened.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Our systems are surely not perfect and there is much that we need to keep doing.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If we are not careful, we may be planting seeds of doubt dan in time, the trust in our systems will be eroded.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is true for all systems and institutions in this country.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If a negative perception spreads, even though it is not based on facts, we will erode the trust of the people towards our systems and institutions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We see many things happening in other countries where the trust in the key institutions of the country has disappeared.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have to ensure that our systems are always clean and transparent, but at the same time, we cannot just wantonly make baseless assumptions and damage people’s trust.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Therefore, although I agree with the call to continue improving any existing shortcoming, I feel that there needs to be a realisation and acknowledgment of the strength of our justice system, the existing continuous effort to increase its standards and the sincerity of the many officers who work in our institutions like the police and prosecutors who carry the responsibility to ensure the efficacy of our system.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I hope we can continue to uphold our existing systems and continue to protect it; and ensure that justice and equality continue to be the key foundations of our country.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: A house is standing because of the joints Which is cared for perfectly and well A nation is strong with a promise That our we guard our values with our hearts (In English): Thank you.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, let me try and deal with specific points but let me start off by saying the speeches I have heard, particularly from the Workers' Party.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Now, I will come back to Mr Leong Mun Wai.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I would say – with the Workers' Party and the points made – we are on the same page.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In many ways, we are pushing at an open door.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is not that any of these principles are new or in some way not thought of or that we are opposed to them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think in large measure, from the speeches that I heard, you are setting out positions of principle, which we have no problems with, but sitting on the front bench here, we also got to decide how to implement it and how to pay for it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And so, therein comes some of the implementation issues.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If I may say, actually, the very first point I will take illustrates that very well.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Legally, I think Ms Lim, Ms He Ting Ru and maybe Mr Dennis Tan talked about the importance of legal aid, particularly for the poor.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Of course, we want legal aid for the poor and we do have legal aid for the poor.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But I have explained why I do not want to make legal aid mandatory.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I explained to you by reference to the UK example – that the moment you make it mandatory, then what happens?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: People game the system too and people game the system in this way.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They will not be able to find lawyers who can do it for the fee that the state is prepared to pay, or an extraordinarily exorbitant fee is required, or lawyers do not come forward.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And because you cannot find the lawyer to handle the case, therefore the case gets postponed.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I gave you real-life examples from a first class jurisdiction – UK.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is not a figment of anyone's imagination.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think rather than going the same paths that others have gone and gotten into minefields, we should try and make it work.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will also share with you – I had it in my original text but I took it out because of the length – the experience of Australia and New Zealand.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: New South Wales in Australia offers a fully government-funded public defender's scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Two thirds of its cases are outsourced to private lawyers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Every time I show these figures, my Finance Minister gives me a look.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Similarly, when we enhanced CLAS in 2014, we were not in a very difficult budgetary position but we were all projecting for a time when we would be in a difficult budgetary position.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I did not want to get into a situation where we will just be required to write bigger and bigger cheques without taking into account public interest.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The reason why any Member here, with a child who is 10 years old, would dare to let their child take public transport is because of our law and order system.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is a privilege – every lady in this room will be able to take public transport at any time of the day and night.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You will not be able to exercise that in any comparable city, anywhere in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There is a reason for all of that.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is because cases get dealt with properly.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have kept crime low at a relatively low cost to the taxpayer.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But I accept we must also help the poor when it comes to legal aid for criminal cases.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He was an experienced lawyer accused of murdering his wife, received legal aid in 2013.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Do you believe that that person should get legal aid at that cost in Singapore?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we should move away from absolutist positions to say, "How can we make it work?", because we are both on the same side on this argument.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Paul Cohrs was accused of murdering his mother and brother in 2018.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He was offered legal aid because his assets were frozen.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Court cases get delayed – I am talking about Australia now – because lawyers refuse to take on legal aid cases.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Legal aid rates were considered inadequate; cases being adjourned.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Victims and witnesses are having to endure a long wait for justice and preparation by prosecutors and the police wasted.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In 2016, court cases against alleged murderers of underworld figures, Barbaro and Yilmaz, were put off for more than one year because legal aid rates were inadequate for suitable lawyers to take on the lengthy and complex case.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The government introduced reforms in 2020 to ensure more sustainable legal aid budgets, including changes in fee structures, introduced fixed-sum lump-sum payments for less serious criminal matters.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There was an independent review of the system in 2009 led by a senior civil servant.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: She concluded the system was open to abuse, including lawyers who game the system.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I am not suggesting that lawyers will necessarily game the system but you have these experiences elsewhere and you got to be careful about it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They delayed plea or changed plea part way through the process, maximised legal aid payments.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Lawyers demanded or accepted top-up payments from clients.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: To curb the bill, they expanded the public defender's scheme but that was also opposed by the bar.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The question is – how do you implement it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, I think there was a question of bail.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think Ms Lim wondered if the Bail Court was comatose or still in existence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Court 4A undertakes the role of the Bail Court.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It handles the grant of, or review of, bail.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Court aims to ensure that the bail reviews are dealt with expeditiously, minimise – we are again on the same page – the time spent by accused persons in remand and balance against the need to ensure that the accused persons attend Court or are available when investigations are required.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, again, on the bail issue, I do not think there is divergence here.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Three, on people who cannot afford to pay fines.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think the situation that Ms Lim highlighted was that some people run up a series of regulatory offences and then they find themselves unable to pay and then have to turn up to Court for these matters.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is a tough issue when it comes to this because, in principle, you have the laws, you need to enforce them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think everybody agrees that you need to enforce them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Because if you have laws and you have fines that can be imposed but if people can break the rules – it can be as simple as parking, if people can park without having to pay the fines and fines will not be collected – then, the system will slowly break down.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But, then, there are a group of people we all feel sympathetic towards because they cannot pay.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The fact that they cannot pay the fines then lead some on to other situations which sort of snowball and we really do not want that.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think that is a situation where other kinds of safety nets will have to come and try and help them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is where MSF comes in, the local Member of Parliament, or MP, comes in, for situations like that.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But where the agencies come across this, some agencies may be able to handle it but, generally, the agencies are not best placed to go and make distinctions between people – okay, you can pay the fine, you cannot pay the fine.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think we will very soon have a system that is dysfunctional.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think that sort of intervention has got to be an intervention from outside of the regulatory agency.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But, in principle, we agree that there must be ways to try and find these people help.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ms Lim also talked about how AGC sometimes – I am sure this is based on what the criminal bar has said because they have said this to me too – that officers sometimes prefer the most serious charge.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think in the Parliament, when we debate like this, it is going to be general statements.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you say they should not put the most serious charge, of course, I agree.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But we also agree that neither the Parliament nor MinLaw should be directing AGC on what charges are appropriate.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think the starting point is what the Attorney-General has said at the Opening of Legal Year, which is that the DPPs ought to be told, and have been told, they are ministers of justice.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They need to take an overview on this and they need to approach this with fairness.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Attorney-General and the Deputy Attorney-General have regular discussions with the criminal bar.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Recording of statements – again, I think the starting point is the same.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It must be fair to the person being interviewed.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It must be something that the person who is interviewed can understand.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I do not think it is going to be possible – the Police are not going to be able to record it in the language the witness speaks.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we need to have the right interpreter and we must emphasise to the IOs that – look, it is not a question of getting down and putting it in the way that you want.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It has got to be what the person is saying.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I am sure Ms Lim has, I am sure others have – I have – we have all come across situations where lawyers tell us – well, the statement has been taken in a way that is not quite accurate.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think you have got to discount some of it because it is seen from a defence's perspective.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, this is something, as I said, the golden standard would be if we can have video recording but in my Ministerial Statement, I explained, or in my clarifications, I explained the difficulties that we are having.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Not that we do not want to do it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is protective of the Police but we cannot do it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We cannot expand it because of the specific resource constraints that I spoke about.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There was a question on the level of legal training of IOs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: None of that is going to make them a lawyer and, I think, again, the real answer is what one of the Members asked me earlier – how quickly can we put the AGC and Police officers together early in the investigations so that there is that legal guidance?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The size of the Police's IOs is small.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: To try and put them together to deal with these thousands of cases, is not going to be easy.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In my original statement, I actually said I am personally very sympathetic to the IO.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Police were very uncomfortable with that because they take the disciplinary inquiry seriously and their view was that if the Minister says that, then it creates difficulties for them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But I am very sympathetic to the IO because we are all looking at this with hindsight and with a huge microscope, day by day.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He did not do it for five weeks.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ms Lim also asked about instalment payments for fines.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have said it in the House here.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think we should try when people have difficulties in making payments to allow them to pay in instalments.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The difficulty again is to distinguish between who can afford and who cannot afford.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There were some points about young people, what sort of assistance they get when Police interview them, amongst others.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Actually, for those who have not been following closely our criminal justice system and our system of imprisonment or incarceration, there has been a sea change in approach.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Today, for example, the Prisons service tags itself as Captains of Lives.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When the people come in, the statistics show that there is a high likelihood of recidivism when they go out.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, our task is to actually be with them and make sure as much as possible that they do not come back.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We do a lot of intervention when they are in there.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We actually want to go earlier, upstream, do not even let them become prisoners, do not even let them get into trouble.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And we want to look as much as possible, for people who infringe or who have committed some offence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We want to see how we can move them away from the penal system to a more guidance programme for rehabilitation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, the primary focus, if I can use one word to describe our system today, it is to focus on rehabilitation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Which is why the very significant changes on first- and second-time drug users were put through legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, for young people, we have diversionary programmes for those who commit minor offences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We also have a guidance programme for young offenders who commit less serious sexual offences, like possession of obscene films and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Streetwise Programme is a voluntary programme for wayward young people.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For those involved in minor gang-related offences, they are sent to these programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our approach today is first, we try and prevent them from getting into Prison.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, if they commit some offence, as far as possible, we put them in different tracks.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Even if they have to serve time, then, we see whether they have to serve the full time or whether they can be put through different programmes and then, put in halfway houses to the extent possible – of course, depending on the nature of the offence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, that has been the approach and if Members are interested, we can give them a specific, more in-depth briefing.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But there has been a very significant change in approach here.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ms Lim talked about victims in a couple of specific cases.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ms Lim, Ms He Ting Ru will accept, I do not know the facts, I do not know why specifically the matter was not proceeded with.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: All I know from what has been said in Parliament is that AGC advised that it cannot be proceeded with.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Beyond that, I do not know anything else and I cannot comment on it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are always two sides to every story and we will have to ask AGC why it did not proceed.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ms He said that defence lawyers face unequal access to witnesses and evidence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Again, in principle, I agree there should be fair access.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What is fair, how do you detail what is fair, there might be a difference of views.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It was not quite clear to me what exactly she said.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But I am setting out a matter of principle here.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Access to counsel, I have dealt with earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But on a regular basis, if every case, the state loses, you have got to pay compensation, then, I think I would take a different approach and a different view.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I do think that would create chilling effect on prosecution.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But I do not think that is what Ms He was suggesting.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Dennis Tan expressed his concern about the young and the poor.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I say for the record, we are all concerned.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Dennis Tan is not the only one who is concerned.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think his concern is legitimate but we are all concerned.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He also spoke about judicial training and he spoke about this point about rotation between the different parts of the Legal Service.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have given a very full answer and I have said that these matters are dealt with by various boards headed by the Chief Justice.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He decides, together with his board, and there is, I described the Personnel Board for Judges and Personnel Board for Legal Service Officers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Tan also spoke about qualifications of Judicial Officers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These are matters for the Legal Service Commission.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I told you about the Judicial Personnel Board.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think he got some of his facts wrong.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: All are qualified persons who are at least seven years.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I stand corrected – these are the figures I have been given.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If it is inaccurate in any way, I will let Mr Dennis Tan know.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And training of Judicial Officers, again, I agree with Mr Tan, and it is already being done, as he will probably know – Singapore Judicial College.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And Mr Tan agrees that this is a good development.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Pritam Singh talks about disclosure, setting up a statutory framework on what needs to be disclosed.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think specific on Kadar vs Public Prosecutor, Mr Singh would recall, that I told this House that it is good in principle, the Kadar case, and should be followed.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Maybe Mr Singh does not recall, but that is what I said.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, the Government is absolutely ad idem with Mr Singh on this point.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It has started with MHA; it is being discussed.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think it is unsatisfactory that it is left as a common law principle.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we are going to put it out in statute – what is appropriate, what is fair, how do you framework it, which are the cases and principles you take.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is being discussed with various stakeholders; we have not discussed with the bar yet.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think we have discussed it with Supreme Court, I cannot remember specifically.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It has been something that we have been discussing since early this year.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But this small event of COVID-19 has put many of these things out of kilter.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, a little bit more time is being taken.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Singh also talked about how do counsel discuss relevance and non-relevance.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think all I can say to him is, AGC officers have an over-arching duty as ministers of justice.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Singh and I cannot be telling them what to disclose and what not to disclose.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Again, as I have said, we will put it out in statutory form.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, he is pushing at an open door on this.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ms Lim talked about more means for seeking compensation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think she knows 2010, we amended the CPC to require the Courts to actively consider.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Because we felt that while we had given the Courts the power to order compensation, we did not see enough cases where compensation was being awarded.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Rather than requiring the victims to start another proceedings, decide then and there how much money should be paid.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But if for some reason, you think that no money ought to be paid, you set out your reasons.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, victims will be able to participate in the process by making submissions.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The criminal Courts are not equipped to deal with complex hearings which are dealt with by civil Courts.
