speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And we also should be careful about dragging out proceedings because there is a knock-on effect on the Courts’ ability to deal with other cases.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Courts have also been empowered to order compensation to the dependants of a person whose death was caused by an offence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, those are the points I wanted to cover.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are other points which I am sure some other colleagues will cover.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Coming back to Mr Leong Mun Wai and the Committees of Inquiry, he will recall the earlier exchange.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He has agreed that there was no issue he could identify and there was no need for a Committee of Inquiry, or a Commission of Inquiry.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But now, he has reversed himself and says, I suppose an hour or so in between, has helped him to recall why he wanted it in the first place.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Leong, let me put it this way.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You are quite wrong in saying this is an internal review by agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, it has gone through a very public process with detailed cross-examination and an examination in the minute, a forensic examination of all the issues.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Every possible issue relating to the Police, and AGC, and the evidence has been dealt with in great detail in public, in cross-examination and in submissions.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, what is it that you want from a review that has not been publicly set out?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Then, you have a High Court Judge who sets out his judgment and has set out what he said were the issues.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, you have got a judgment from a High Court, setting out, “This is where I felt that Police were lacking and this is where I think the AGC was lacking”.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we had that process, which is, I think he would accept, an independent process.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Next, as regard to AGC, that is going to go for another Disciplinary Tribunal.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the officers will give account of what they did.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It will be dealt with by the Disciplinary Tribunal or DT, and if the DT feels that there is a case to answer and it needs to be referred, it goes up to the Court of Three Judges.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Or the DT dismisses it – whatever it is, that is another independent inquiry.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, that deals with the AGC part of your requirement for the Commission of Inquiry.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Three specific issues were identified: translation and two other issues.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have dealt with them, the three issues.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will answer your other points, but perhaps I can invite you to answer that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: When we look at this case, basically, it is a case where there are a number of possible systematic faults across this case.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: For example, from the Police to the AGC – you admitted there were lapses.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And the AGC, there is a case that is still in the Courts now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And now, you have also disclosed or have said that the behaviour of some of the plaintiffs is not credible.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If there are so many of these problems, at every stage of the process, there is supposed to be a check on the problem.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The way I listened to what you have said, now it seems that the problem is like being drilled down to a poor guy in the Police force.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If one person makes a mistake, the next stage of the process is supposed to check on that and then stop the mistake from carrying on.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, to a layman like me – as I have said, I am not a legal expert – and probably the average Singaporean in society, we will think that, eh, the whole process, why nothing stops this process from carrying on, making the poor Ms Liyani suffer for four years?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I could ask you, Mr Leong, I have heard about the four years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will come back to the four years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, what is it that requires the commission of inquiry?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We think that the systemic failures that I have—

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The systemic failure is like what I have explained just now – why, in the process, was there no stopper?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, if this poor policeman makes the wrong investigation—

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Basically, from the Police, it went on to the AGC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It did not go on to anyone else.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: AGC issue, where it happened at trial, will be dealt with by a Disciplinary Tribunal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, what is it about the Police – beyond the five weeks?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: You actually mentioned that there were some lapses in the treatment of the evidence.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: When this five-week thing happened, why did the superior officer in the Police force, for example, not identify the problem?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And when this moved to AGC to make the prosecution—

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have told you that the IO and the supervisor were wrong and will be dealt with by way of a Disciplinary Tribunal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What is that you propose – what is your allegation?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Are you suggesting that they did not do it because of improper influence?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If so, say it and we will have a commission of inquiry.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I am not saying that that is definitely the case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Okay, then tell me why we need a commission of inquiry.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Like what I have said, Minister, if a junior officer had done something, why was it not checked by a senior officer, and then the senior officer—

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The senior officer is now going to face a Disciplinary Inquiry, too.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Then this senior officer made a mistake, this whole thing goes to AGC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There was a lapse, unless we are suggesting or we have reason to believe.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In any system – and you have been in organisations – there will be lapses.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Lapses do not equate to Commissions of Inquiry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Commission of inquiry is if there is something larger.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You are not suggesting – it is good that you have disavowed any suggestion of improper influence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, once we accept that, then the question is, on these facts—and I have told you 10% of the cases succeed on appeal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have told you there is another case where there was a break in the chain of custody.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We cannot be having Commissions of Inquiry each time the High Court says that the Police have made a mistake.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the reason why I was prepared to recommend a commission of inquiry was because I felt your suggestion was Mr Liew had improper influence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, therefore, in terms of how the Police handled it, the two officers – maybe more than two, or whether there were other IOs who have dealt with it at different times – that is a matter for the Police.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And you would have heard me saying I welcome Ms Sylvia Lim's point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we do not need a commission of inquiry.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Like you said just now, Minister, in an organisation, when we do a cross-department investigation, sometimes, in the organisation when things like, for example, the Operations Department makes a mistake and the Finance Department—

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This inquiry internally was done by the CID, which is external to the IOs, and the next level of disciplinary proceedings will also be done properly and I did say to Mr Pritam Singh, if he was interested, I will let him know what the results are.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I need to go and check the law as to whether I am entitled to tell him.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I think you will be good enough to agree that if those are the concerns, there is no basis for a commission of inquiry?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now I am left with nothing else to answer.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Then we do not need the Leader now.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I have two clarifications for Minister on what he has just said.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The first clarification concerns his response to my suggestion on the recording of statements in languages other than English.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I wanted to highlight that other countries have done it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I hope that he will not close his mind to the matter.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And if this could be done – that means, recording the text of the statement in a language other than English – I think that would greatly increase reliability.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The second clarification is what he mentioned in response to my point on the victims.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The two cases which I have mentioned, of course, I am not expecting the Government to comment on the merits of the cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: My reason for bringing them up is to highlight that no reasons were given to the victims for the decisions made and, more generally, to advocate for greater recognition in the Singapore system of the role of victims as stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And based on these two cases – and there are many others as well – it is clear that victims do feel disempowered and I think we can do better to recognise their role as stakeholders in the system.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not really have a quarrel with either point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I have expressed the hope we are waiting for artificial intelligence and video-to-text automatically.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have looked at some, but they are not yet mature technologies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the second point of the role of victims as stakeholders, I think Ms Sylvia Lim would have heard me say, in fact, I have pushed for that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we will see where else the right role of victims can be better protected.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Is the Minister saying that jurisdiction with more legal aid or a more beefed-up legal aid system will lead to bad outcomes?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Are there not ways that we can expand our system or having safeguards to make sure that the abuses that he cited do not happen and that costs do not spiral out of control?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I was corrected by the Prime Minister that I had mispronounced your name.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the answer to both questions is, no, I am not saying any of those things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, I said we are on the same page.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we need to avoid those traps, but try and achieve the objective in a way that will make the Finance Minister reasonably comfortable.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My second posting in the Legal Service was at AGC.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This involved significant decisions whether or not to prosecute a person or to charge a person.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One of the cases I had prosecuted was to do with rioting.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The facts of the case were that there appeared to be a riot in a foreign worker dormitory.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Things got tense and people started to fight.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But I was not sure whether one of them was even part of the fight.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a DPP, I raised the question to my superior that rather than being part of the fight, I thought that the foreign worker in question was trying to break up the fight.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I was instructed to interview the foreign worker.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I asked to do a site visit where the fight happened, in order to get a sense of the evidence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That, to me, was my experience of the AGC – the integrity of the AGC.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is so easy to tar an institution, but I feel that, on the whole, AGC is an excellent institution, made up of good officers and I want to stand up and say that today.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the example I gave, the foreign worker did not have a defence counsel.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, the decision-making was all borne on the shoulders of the DPPs in question and the superiors we reported to.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One has to appreciate within AGC the intense nature of the work, the huge number of investigation papers, evidence and statements, and on top of that, having to run trials, attend plea of guilt mentions and pre-trial conferences.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is tough work, as Minister Shanmugam said, it is dynamic.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is so many pressures and each decision has sometimes life or liberty of a person in question.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The second point, Sir, I would like to make is that a lot has been said about the trial Judge who handled the case at first instance in the State Courts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here, I would also like to speak up for the system and see that there is indeed a lot of pressure on Judges.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Then, the Judge needs to ask if indeed the person is guilty.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How does one tamper justice with mercy in a sentence?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And in sentencing, there can be so many permutations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Again, I say this in this House with some level of experience – notwithstanding that experience as a very junior judicial officer – my first posting in the Legal Service, before AGC.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Judge could be guided by retribution, which is a form of punishment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Or the Judge can be guided by deterrence which is to deter the accused or others from doing the same offence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Or a judge could opt for rehabilitation because he or she sees the sincerity in the offender and feels that he or she should be given a second chance to rehabilitate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Or the Judge can opt for restorative justice – which is my favourite type of justice – where the offender is given a chance to apologise for his or her mistakes and the relationship is restored between the accused and the victim.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, in addition to needing to weigh up evidence, that is, whether the person is guilty beyond reasonable doubt or whether he or she should be acquitted, the Judge needs to decide what rationale of sentencing to apply.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is not easy and we have many excellent State Court Judges.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We will never be finished trying to improve the system.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One listens to the Minister and all the speeches – we are all trying to improve the system, yes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But we have got a good foundation here.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And there have been significant policy improvements over the years which I am aware of as counsel in private practice – which I declare to you, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have expanded the criminal case disclosure regime by having access to more information, the defence would be able to better prepare a more accurate case.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have allowed video recorded statements to be adduced as verbal evidence under certain circumstances to reduce the trauma of vulnerable victims.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have introduced provisions allowing certain vulnerable victims to testify, shielded from the accused.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, we do have a good system, Sir.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This particular case has shown that there are still areas for improvement and I am heartened that the agencies will be reflecting on this case.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have every confidence that we can continue working from a good solid base towards a fair justice system for all.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It may need improving, but it is a good system nonetheless.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many of the problems they face will be in addition to those faced by low-income Singaporeans, which my Workers' Party's colleagues in this House have highlighted.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, I would like to discuss the challenges faced by migrant workers who are victims of abuse, salary non-payment or other offences.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Migrant workers face steep power imbalances when dealing with employers and Government authorities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They are in a foreign land and may not speak our local languages well.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They are far from their families and their friends back home.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some migrant domestic workers do not even have a local support network because they have limited interaction with peers outside of their employers' homes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They are unfamiliar with our local laws and customs and often do not know their rights.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: She was sent back to Indonesia just as she was due for a medical check-up and chose not to tell the immigration officers of the abuse as she was happy to finally escape it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It was only when she returned to her village in Indonesia that her family discovered her injuries and made a report.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Migrant workers in these situations are often caught between a rock and a hard place.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If they choose not to report the wrongdoing, it may continue or their perpetrators may get away scot-free.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If they choose to report the offence and their case is taken up by the authorities, they will have to remain in Singapore to assist in the investigations and cannot immediately return to their loved ones at home.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By the time the final sentence is passed, the entire process may have taken two years or more.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In the meantime, the worker may not be able to work to earn a living.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This can be financially ruinous as they are often the sole breadwinners of a large family back home.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They are still required to seek permission from the investigating authorities before working.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Fortunately, in most cases, permission is granted for victims.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many employers may be hesitant to employ migrant domestic workers who are assisting in Police investigations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some victims may be so traumatised by the abuse that they do not wish to risk being in such a dangerous situation again.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They also have to look for a place to stay.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The burden of sheltering them currently falls mainly on non-government organisations or NGOs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Taking a step back, there are other factors which may give migrant workers great pause before they make a brave move to report their abuse.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, many come from countries where corruption and abuse of authority is rife.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could make them inherently distrustful of authorities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some may even need to be assured that Police officers in Singapore will not demand a bribe to take up their case.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, the employers may sometimes make or threaten to make counter-accusations against them, for example, accusing them of theft or damaging company property.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Third, in cases where there is no physical abuse, but strong elements of coercion or psychological abuse, the investigation might end with a warning but no punishment for the employers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In all of these cases, the end result for the worker would likely be termination of their current employment and repatriation to their home countries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The cost of premature repatriation is tremendous for these workers to find work in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They would have incurred thousands of dollars of debts owed to recruitment agents in their home countries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They would have to spend months, sometimes years, paying off these debts on the back up low salaries in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Being terminated and terminated and sent home will saddle them with huge debts, not to mention a loss of income and embarrassment for their families.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: At the end of the whole trial, even if the perpetrator is convicted, the victim may not be financially compensated for the full extent of what they had suffered.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I will now move on to the challenges faced by migrant workers accused of crimes while in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Her recorded statements were read back to her in English and translated into Bahasa Melayu by the Investigation Officer or IO.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: No Bahasa Indonesia interpreter was present for the recording of four of her statements.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: During cross-examination in Court, the IO conceded that there was a difference between Bahasa Melayu and Bahasa Indonesia, and admitted that he could have understood Ms Liyani's statements in Bahasa Indonesia differently from what she had meant.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Justice Chan Seng Onn, in his judgment, also said that the likelihood similarly existed that Ms Liyani could have misunderstood the IO's questions during the interview and recorded statements read back to her differently from what the IO had meant.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: He was thus satisfied that there was a reasonable doubt in relation to the accuracy of the translation for two of the statements.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Accused workers also need to remain in Singapore to assist with investigations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Most migrant workers accused of crimes may not be able to secure such a bailar.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They faced a similar dilemma as victims when deciding whether to plead guilty or claim trial.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Should they plead guilty, the time it takes for them to serve their sentence may be shorter than the time it takes to go through the Court process if they claim trial.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Even if they know that they are innocent, bizarrely, it is actually expedient for the migrant worker to plead guilty even if they did no wrong.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Should they claim trial, they may not find a lawyer and will certainly not be able to afford one.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Criminal legal aid is available but not by default as they need to pass means and merits test.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Even if they do, they may still not be able to find a lawyer willing to take up their case pro bono.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: My Liyani was very fortunate to have a Singaporean lawyer, Mr Anil Balchandani, representing her pro bono at the trial and the appeal.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Justice Chan commended Mr Anil for showing much skill and dedication in his work for this case.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I would now like to share some proposals on how we can make the justice system fairer for migrant workers who have to go through it, either as victims or accused persons.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, we have to tackle the upstream problems, which severely hamper their bargaining power vis-a-vis their employers and contribute to their unwillingness to report abuse.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We must find ways to reduce the high recruitment fees that migrant workers need to pay agents to find a job in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If workers do not feel such a sense of obligation to their employer because of a need to pay back exorbitant fees to recruiters, they will be more likely to report abuse when it happens.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I shared one solution to this during September's debate on the President's Address – to create a jobs portal that advertises all open positions for migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The positions should be open to only Singaporeans for a period of, say, two weeks before being extended to foreigners.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: With increasing IT savviness, migrant workers can even search for such positions from their home countries and apply directly.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This move towards jobs transparency would cut out the middleman and reduce the need to pay exploitative fees to recruitment agents.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, support services should be provided to all workers who choose to make complaints against employers and find themselves without a home and a job.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It should not be left entirely to NGOs and their limited resources.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This support should include the provision of basic needs like food and shelter, counselling services and help on understanding their rights.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Third, every individual, local or foreign, should have access to legal representation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If they cannot afford a lawyer, legal aid should be made available to them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To prevent abuse, means testing could be done so that only those who are in genuine need will have their legal fees covered.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I note that Minister said earlier that the public defender's office is under consideration.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I welcome this and I hope that this will be pursued further.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And fourth, once the Court orders a payment of compensation to the victim, the system must ensure that the victim receives that payment.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Victims should not be left high and dry, just because the convicted person is unable to pay.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If necessary, a fund could be set up to ensure that victims are guaranteed to receive the compensation amount ordered by the Court.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In 2014, the AGC announced that it had formed an internal working group to focus on improving Court processes involving abused migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It mentions several areas it was looking at, including: one, exploring how to help more foreign maids get compensation for the losses they incur after they stop working because of abuse; two, improving Court processes involving abused foreign workers; three, securing medical reports and witness statements more quickly; four, persuading the Courts to fix early hearing dates; and five, expanding the use of compensation orders to help more maids obtain compensation for losses resulting from a criminal offence committed against them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It has been six years since this announcement.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And what were their final proposals and which of them have been implemented?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Even though they are foreigners, they are an integral part of our society – looking after our children and elderly and building our skyscrapers and roads.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As a developed country, it is our duty to ensure that they have equal access to justice if they suffer abuse or are accused of wrongdoing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is crucial that our justice system does not merely provide for its reliability, but actually be perceived to be so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This fence divides the city of Nogales in the State of Sonora, from the city of Nogales in the State of Arizona.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Up until the First World War, Nogales was essentially one city.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In 1918, armed conflict between the army and militia led to the construction of the first permanent border.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Despite the shared history, culture and geography, the fate of those who lived on either side of the Nogales fence could not have been more different.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In Arizona, household incomes amount to about $30,000 a year, most teenagers are in school and life expectancy is relatively high by global standards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Residents are able to go about their daily activities with little fear for their lives or their property.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet just a few feet away, in Sonora, however, most teenagers do not complete high school and most adults do not possess a high school certificate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Health conditions are poor with mothers worrying about the survival of their infants.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And in contrast to their neighbours in the north, the rule of law is weak, with endemic crime and significant risks involved in the starting and running of businesseses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This story, retold by economist Daron Acemoglu and political scientist James Robinson in their book "Why Nations Fail", underscores the importance of legal, political institutions, such as the rule of law in shaping economic outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In particular, the authors argue that when institutions are inclusive, when decision-making is shared by many and the system is subject to robust checks and balances, human flourishing is allowed the room it needs to succeed, thereby bringing progress and prosperity for nations that subscribe to such quality institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Singapore has historically distinguished Itself by being an island, literally and figuratively, of institutional stability in a sea of tumultuous institutional change.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As a Crown Colony, we inherited a sophisticated legal system and chose to adhere to this conception of the rule of law following Independence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This choice has generally served us well, both from the perspective of natural justice and because the rule of law has been an important cornerstone that has underpinned our business and commercial activities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We must guard against taking this inheritance for granted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Globally, the rule of law is in retreat.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The World Bank's Governance Indicators also document an erosion in the rule of law since 1996 for developed and developing countries alike.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Countries in Central Europe have experienced particularly marked declines in their adherence to the rule of law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Closer to our neighbourhood, a number of nations in ASEAN have also experienced reductions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Although as Minister Shanmugam has argued, Singapore remains highly ranked, we sadly have not been exempt from this trend.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We have seen a decline in indicators of the rule of law over time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, the different measures of the rule of law are often constructed from the reported perceptions of the public and society at large, of the quality of their day-to-day interactions of citizens with the legal system, their sense of whether contracts are enforced, whether property rights are respected and whether the police and judges are trustworthy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is why careful reviews such as what this Motion is calling for, are so important because they can restore the confidence of the public in the inherent fairness of the legal process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The objective is to ensure that there is a consistency between the intent of the existing laws on the books, what is sometimes referred to as the jury system, and the perceptions of how the law is practised, the de facto system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If the gap in perceptions becomes too large, the rule of law risks becoming disconnected and hence, discounted by the public to the detriment of more than just justice per se.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is precisely why so many Members in this House have discussed the importance that the rule of law not just be done but be perceived to be done.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Now, when the rule of law is compromised, economic performance suffers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is abundant empirical evidence that asserts this relationship.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Put simply, when people are insecure about the rule of law, they invest less, they produce less; and even when they work and invest, they are less productive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We watch movies on LG and Samsung TVs and smart phones, and many of us, including my dear mother and sister, go crazy over Kpop and Korean TV dramas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: With that parting thought, I assert my support for the Motion.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With that in mind, I have some proposals that I believe will help strengthen our criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many of what I will share has been discussed previously, but I hope to share further points in detail on some of these proposals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The scheme allows an independent and trained adult to accompany vulnerable groups who have to give statements to the Police.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is meant to ensure that the vulnerable person is not misunderstood during the interview.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It makes sense to also include FDWs into the scheme.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, when we recently raised penalties for crimes against vulnerable people, we did specifically include FDWs as a class of vulnerable people.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I completely understand the tremendous workload of our Police officers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, may I suggest that MHA work with the NGOs for this and it might help ease the workload a little.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I would be glad to help facilitate this process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is about video recording, and Minister has addressed this point significantly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Hopefully, this can take place sooner rather than later.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The key words here are "in their own language", which is used in the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC) in some sections.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It states that people who do not understand English should be provided interpretation in a language they understand.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It provides no clarity on what is the standard of "understanding" and who gets to determine it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I propose that we set high but reasonable standards for language interpretation during Police interviews.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, all Police interviews start with the Investigation Officer (IO) informing suspects that they can request for an interpreter.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They should get to declare what this language is and this should be officially recorded.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, the interpreter should have professional certification or relevant experience to ensure their services rendered are of suitable quality.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Fourth, new rules should be introduced to mandate that interpreters follow certain protocols.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For one, they should stick strictly to interpretation and avoid providing any legal advice or personal inputs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Programmes could be set up to accredit interpreters who receive training in this regard.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Sixth, the interpreter should arrive with minimal delay.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Otherwise, a suspect may accept the absence of an interpreter to avoid being detained for an unduly long period of time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Seventh, the interpreter should not only translate the final statement, but also interpret what the Police officers and the suspect say.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some of these points were addressed by Minister Shanmugam earlier and I am glad he has stated that some changes will be made.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I hope that all the points I have raised above will also be considered.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we cannot have a situation where Police questions can be misunderstood, and we cannot allow suspects the opportunity to later claim that they had misunderstood questions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the grand scheme of things, the cost of interpretation is a small price to pay for the procurement of justice.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One, the introduction of the Appropriate Adult Scheme for foreign domestic workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Two, the mandatory video recording of all Police interviews.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Three, the mandatory provision of language interpretation during Police interviews, with high standards set to ensure professional quality, prompt availability and no misunderstanding.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Time and again, we have seen cases turn on the uncertainty of what happens in the interview room.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When this occurs, it does a disservice to suspects, Police officers, prosecutors, judges and all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But I would say in response to Mr Perera to look at the request in the context not only of the countries that he has cited – and I will come back to that in a moment – but also, particularly, in the context of Singapore – our system, our institutions and our people.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The intention behind the ombudsman is to enhance the rule of law, improve our criminal justice system and I think you have heard earlier Members from this side of the House brook no dissent with that.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We all agree that that is a fundamental objective.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We want to enhance our rule of law.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But I would suggest, Mr Speaker, that the proof of the pudding is really in the eating, in looking not only at the countries that have set up the ombudsman, but to look at where they stand after years, if not decades, of having the ombudsman and the impact it has had on their legal system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, in that respect, we have heard the World Justice Report cited several times.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And if you look more closely at the most recent Crime Index 2020, Malaysia, the Philippines and Indonesia are all behind Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, I would suggest that instead of just citing these experiences from other countries, to put it in the context of where this system operates and the people that operate the system as well, and ask ourselves, what is that reality?

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: How does the Ombudsman translate into a better legal system, better rule of law and, fundamentally, a safer Singapore?

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Where would you choose to bring up children?

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Where would you want to have our women and children be safe late at night – in Singapore or some other countries?

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And I think that is the proof of the pudding.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Proof of the pudding is in the eating and that is what I meant when I said that.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And in Singapore, we have our public institutions with its governance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have internal reviews and, to the extent that some Members have said internal reviews are not sufficient because they are all conducted by internal people, then, on occasion, where necessary, there is the external review as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I am sure Mr Perera is aware of the fact that there are many such panels.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In MHA, there is the independent Review Panel set up to review cases externally, independently.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The SAF has set up external Review Panels as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And to the extent that issues of public interest are raised, there is this forum in Parliament, and I am sure Members will agree that as we sit here past 10 pm this evening, that we spare no effort debating, discussing, going down into every detail that matters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Members will remember that we have had the SingHealth breach raised in Parliament as well by way of Ministerial Statements, by way of Parliamentary Questions; the MRT breakdown, the MINDEF incidents, even what happens to doctors when they are apparently wrongly prosecuted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And on occasion, even that may not be enough.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And after the recent SCDF incidents were ventilated in Parliament, a separate Board of Inquiry, or BOI, was set up to look into the matter, separate from the Police investigation, came up with a report which subsequently MHA accepted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On top of all of these, we have the COI.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have had a lot of debate about the COI, whether it is "committee" or "commission".

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But that provides an additional layer with public hearings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I am not suggesting that these numbers are high or low.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But I think where it needs to happen, this is an avenue.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is an avenue that our citizens can avail themselves of: bring their claims and the Courts – not the Executive, not an internal body – will evaluate these claims.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And, ultimately, when you have an ombudsman, the question really is: can they serve a better function than each of these specialist panels set up specifically for an inquiry, where necessary, with the relevant powers of investigation and with the relevant expertise for each of these cases?

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Perera said CPIB only investigates corruption, but not rude behaviour.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have the Members of Parliament who listen to residents every week, week in, week out.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I am sure many of you would have come across occasions where you were told so and so was rude to me, so and so did not listen to me.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There are proper avenues for this to be brought up.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, I would say to Mr Perera and to other Members suggesting the ombudsman, to look at this suggestion in the context of not only what we have in our society already running, functioning, but also what the end result has shown.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Police report was lodged on 30 October 2016 and Members will remember that Ms Liyani returned to Singapore in December 2016.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: She was then arrested and, for a period of time, the Police conducted their investigations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On 5 June 2017, the Police sent the file to AGC for their investigations and recommendations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: AGC asked the Police to clarify certain points, which the Police then looked into.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, counsel said that he could not take dates in February or March 2018.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As a consequence, the trial was fixed for hearing in April 2018.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The verdict by the State Courts was delivered on 20 March 2019 and Ms Liyani was sentenced a few days later on 25 March.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: She then appealed against the sentence and conviction.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will probably sit here past 11 pm as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I am wondering if the Minister is making the argument that having an ombudsman actually lowers the quality of justice, and is there any evidence to that effect?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Is the Minister also saying that all countries that have an ombudsman, generally, because of some causative effect of having an ombudsman, actually fare more poorly in terms of justice indicators and so on and so forth?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I do not think he is, but I do want to clarify that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Would the Minister acknowledge the possibility that those countries, without an ombudsman system, may actually fare even lower in the rankings than where they currently are at?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Thirdly, I believe that the Minister would argue that we have fundamentally strong criminal justice institutions and so on, but I would like to invite the Minister to agree with me that even though things are good, there is a possibility that they can be better.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Would he agree that ideas like the ombudsman may help us to get to that goal?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Lastly, just very briefly, to respond to the Minister's point on QSM and Meet-the-People sessions, I did address that in my speech.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Just look at the NHS ombudsman in the UK and the police ombudsman in the UK.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And we have our system that works in the way in which I have outlined.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I am not sure if I did justice to it when I outlined it very quickly, in the interest of time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I am sure the Member will agree that you have to apply suggestions in the context of what you already have in your own systems and look at whether that is going to improve the system or whether that would create yet another layer.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On his final point, I think we all agree that if we can better the system – obviously – and I think on that, we are on the same page.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: My apologies, the long sitting is affecting my eyesight.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, fellow Members of Parliament: I have heard many speeches and questions from fellow Members.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: While there are differences in opinion, what is clear is that all Members are concerned about this issue and for our country.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In fact, the debate in Parliament today fully reflects the three pillars of our transparent, fair, and structured system of governance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: One, it represents a kind of insistence, an insistence on accountability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Two, it represents our two core values: justice, and equality.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Three, it represents the separation of the three branches of power in Government, that is, the independence of the Legislature, the Executive and the Judiciary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: One, two and three: one insistence, two core values, and three independent branches of Government.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These three key points form the cornerstones of our system of governance, and are implemented across our management and decision-making, across every Public Service Department and every public servant, and in every decision everyone here, makes every day.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Without accountability, we will become a society where people accuse one another and problems remain unresolved; without justice and equality, we will become a corrupt and backward country; without separation of powers, the consequences will be most frightening, and the power vacuum will plunge our country into chaos and crisis.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is certainly not an outcome we want.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To ensure Singapore's continued growth and prosperity, we must hold steadfast to these three pillars of governance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Every job has a certain scope of duty, rules and regulations that must be observed, and tasks that must be done.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: If mistakes are made at work, it is clear that the jobholder must bear responsibility and face the consequences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is the system of accountability that we have always upheld, and this is especially important in the Public Service.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is because the Public Service uses public resources, and thus has to be accountable to the state, to the people, about the areas where resources were used, why they were used, and to produce results.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Public Service has always been open and transparent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: If a civil servant’s performance is unsatisfactory, he/she is held accountable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: If punishment is necessary, it is not shirked, and it is not perfunctory.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The public can see that the assessment system is robust.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: If results are not produced, there are areas of negligence, or laws have been infringed, the jobholder will be promptly removed from the service.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: A holistic, clear, and rational system of accountability encourages us to identify problems, find solutions, and seek progress.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The accountability system should not lead to inaction in the public service, nor should it become a tool for political criticism.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As we identify problems and explore solutions, we must also guard against over-correcting or putting the cart before the horse.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: If a law or judicial process is taken advantage of by criminals to exonerate themselves, or causes people to stop reporting crimes and lose confidence in the justice system, it will go against the objectives and spirit of the original legislation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Second, our two core values of justice and equality.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Justice and equality are the core values on which Singapore depends for her survival.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: They are reflected in our policies in various areas, such as free education for 10 years, ensuring that every Singaporean child has the opportunity to upgrade themselves through education, and thereafter to continue training and maintain job competitiveness through government subsidies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Public housing policies ensure that every resident can afford to own their home, rather than allowing the market to freely determine housing prices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In healthcare, the Government also gives higher subsidies to the low-income and disadvantaged groups, and ensures that every Singaporean has access to quality medical care through Medisave and other schemes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The values of justice and equality have been ingrained in our thinking and systems, as well as our lives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: During the debate on the President’s Address in Parliament in 2018, Prime Minister Mr Lee Hsien Loong said that Singapore would not condone ostentatious displays of wealth or discrimination against others, and must always remain vigilant and must not allow elite groups from becoming closed circles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In 2013, the Ministry of Law announced funding for the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme and in 2015, it co-funded the Enhanced Criminal Legal Aid Scheme with the Singapore Law Society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The scheme also encourages practising lawyers to come forward to provide their services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is a commitment by the Government and community organisations to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Protecting Singaporeans' lives and property is an enduring commitment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This year, the police force celebrates 200 years of maintaining law and order in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This achievement, this sense of security, did not come by easily.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Besides the prosperity and development of the country, our people live and work in peace and harmony, and the Singapore Armed Forces and the Home Team – as well as other law enforcement agencies - do their utmost in their duties.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We must all work together and do our utmost to uphold the reputation of a safe city in the world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Minister K Shanmugam also explained in his Ministerial Statement just now that our system of governance and the justice system abide by the rule of law.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: If anyone commits a crime, he would have to face the consequences of a judicial trial, and would not have any special privileges.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Fellow members who know the law have also shared many precedents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Apart from penalties, it is more important for us to be self-disciplined.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: While the law sets the baseline for our conduct, morals and ethical standards should be the ultimate guide of our behaviour.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We often hear the elderly say: “we must pay attention to “propriety” and law.” This means "proprieties" – which include courtesy and etiquette – should take precedence over the law.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We have to abide by the proprieties and law, and not violate the law.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Confucianism advocates the following goals in life: "observe things, gain knowledge, be sincere, be righteous, improve oneself, keep the family together, govern the state, and bring peace to the world ".

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: If every one of us can be sincere, upright, improve oneself and keep the family together, there will be no reason for police officers to come to our doorstep, much less will there be any negative impact on society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Besides managing oneself well, we also need to care for others, especially the disadvantaged groups in society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: If you find that there are people around you who need help, I urge you to inform welfare organisations in the community, raise the difficulties they face, and work together with everyone to solve them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Do not cross onto the wrong side of the law or embark on the road of crime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This, is where we will have to be accountable to ourselves.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We are all Singapore Citizens; I hope everyone will continue to work together to achieve happiness, prosperity, and progress for our nation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Foreign domestic workers help many of our households and families with care-giving and domestic chores, and we value the contribution of foreign domestic workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: MOM has put in place regulatory framework and partnerships with NGOs to protect and take care of our foreign domestic workers in many ways.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This includes provision of adequate food and medical treatment, safe working conditions and adequate daily rest.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Over the years, we have also made several changes to our laws to better safeguard the well-being of foreign domestic workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Complaints against employers who fail to meet their obligations are investigated and errant employers are given appropriate penalties.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For more serious infringements, employers can be prosecuted.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: First-time foreign domestic workers and employers are educated about their rights and responsibilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Such education is done through the mandatory Foreign Domestic Worker Settling-In Programme and the Employers' Orientation Programme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: At the Settling-In Programme, we inform foreign domestic workers of their rights and encourage them to perform their work duties responsibly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We also educate foreign domestic workers on the multiple channels of help available that they can approach and this includes MOM, of course, employer agencies, the NGOs such as Centre for Domestic Employees, the Police and the embassies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: At the Employers' Orientation Programme, we inform employers of their legal responsibilities towards their foreign domestic workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: MOM has also started a programme with the Centre for Domestic Employees to interview first-time foreign domestic workers in their first few months of employment, conducted in their native language.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This interview helps detect any settling-in or adjustment issues, so that the foreign domestic workers and employers can work through and resolve them early.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: NGOs such as Centre for Domestic Employees and Foreign Domestic Worker Association for Social Support and Training, or FAST, run regular clinics with their legal partners for foreign domestic workers who need legal advice.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Foreign domestic workers will be assisted to secure pro bono representation with volunteer lawyers from the Law Society Pro Bono Services and other partnering law firms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ms Parti Liyani was similarly assisted by Legal Aid facilitated by an NGO.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: MOM allows them to remain in Singapore to assist in investigations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: MOM will ensure that they have proper food and housing, and the foreign domestic workers will be allowed to seek employment during this time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In fact, when I visited the Centre for Domestic Employees or CDE, I met several foreign domestic workers who were in the shelter.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: They were actually very grateful that their basic needs were being taken care of.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In their free time, actually, they also interacted and learned about each other's culture and even picked up simple craft.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For foreign domestic workers who call CDE, we also have a vehicle to go and pick them up if they do not know their way.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The vast majority of employers and foreign domestic workers respect their contractual and legal obligations to each other, and many have strong relationships.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We regularly reach out to employers and foreign domestic workers through electronic direct mailers and newsletters to feature best practices and tips on how to develop good working relationships.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Association of Employment Agencies Singapore gives out awards to honour and recognise foreign domestic workers and employers who have maintained healthy long-lasting relationships.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: One of the award winners in 2019 was Ms Somejo.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: She is 59 years old and has worked with her employer for 28 years and looked after her employer's four daughters like her own.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: When Typhoon Haiyan left Ms Somejo's family homeless in 2013, her employer and one of her daughters raised funds to help Ms Somejo's family rebuild their home.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: A healthy and strong working relationship requires the cooperation and effort of both employers and the foreign domestic workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: MOM will continue to work with the stakeholders to protect the well-being of foreign domestic workers as well as the employers, and promote harmonious relationships between them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We have made good progress through the years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: There is more that we can do and we look forward to working with the stakeholders to improve the system for foreign domestic workers and the employers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is clear from the speeches that we have heard that there is broad consensus on much that is touched by the Motion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is broad consensus on the point that fairness, access and independence have been and continue to be cornerstones of Singapore's justice system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is consensus that justice must apply equally to all, irrespective of means or social status.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And I would add that, it should also not matter what one's race, language or religion is.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These are matters for which there is overwhelming consensus not just in this House, but outside this House as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It reflects the founding values of Singapore from Independence – a point I will develop later in my speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As Ms He pointed out, there are constitutional articles where these values are enshrined and against which all other laws and Executive action are void and effective.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Articles such as Article 9 which deals with no deprivation of life or liberty, safe in accordance with law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is also a broad consensus over the fact that whenever there are shortcomings affecting the judicial system, steps must be identified to remedy them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This has been the case before, now and will continue to be the case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, we need to understand the separation of powers within our Constitution which is modelled on the Westminster system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Executive arm of the Government is accountable to this House for the actions of its enforcement officers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Judiciary is an independent arm of the Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He derives his power from an independent constitutional grant.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our apex Court has described his office as a high constitutional office equal to that of the Judiciary.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They are separate processes spelled out in the Constitution and other legislation to hold judicial and prosecuting officers to account in a way that does not compromise the independence of our Judiciary and the Attorney-General's office.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I agree with Ms Lim in her view that the justice system must work fairly for disadvantaged and vulnerable persons navigating the system as defenders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For them, we need to ensure equal access to justice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Access to justice does not necessarily equate to assess to lawyers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These are the words of Lady Hale, the retired President of the UK Supreme Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In Singapore, Courts have taken great pains to explain their decision so that people could understand the law, particularly in the criminal law sphere.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And I would even say, for sentencing the Courts have come up with frameworks to allow people to understand for a certain kind of offence, what would be the probable sentence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This would assist lay people to appreciate what decisions they would face if they were to be convicted in a court of law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But one accepts that a Judge would generally be in a better position to decide on the merits of the case as a neutral umpire hearing both sides, as opposed to entering into the fray to help frame questions and arguments for the unrepresented person.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The main points I wish to make in my speech are as follows.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a country that is governed by the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That has been my experience over the past 28 years as a former regular Police officer and now a lawyer.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hallmark of the rule of law is independence and transparency of the Judiciary.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And I am very glad to note that hon Members from the Workers' Party agree fully with this point.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The second point I wish to make is that in the context of administration of justice that involves more stakeholders; the Police, the DPPs, the State Courts, Judiciary and so on, we have made improvements over time, over years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And today we have heard very good suggestions from both sides of the House which should be considered, debated and distilled.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The point that the hon Minister for Home Affairs made just a few moments ago, is something that we should bear in mind.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With that as a background, I wish to recount my experience in the Police force.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, Ms Lim was my colleague; a very capable colleague, I would add.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The work of the Singapore Police Force officers, then and now, has always been focused on protecting the vulnerable amongst us.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Although it has been decades since I left the force, I can still vividly remember some cases I personally dealt with.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
